articles.title: Palace leaves prosecution to decide on bribery allegations vs Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Malacañang on Sunday said it would leave it to the House prosecution team to decide whether to drop the bribery allegations against Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment case, but warned…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 4:18pm

Malacañang on Sunday said it would leave it to the House prosecution team to decide whether to drop the bribery allegations against Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment case, but warned that doing so could leave Filipinos without answers.

“Nasa pagpapasya po iyan ng prosecution. Kung sa tingin nila ay iyan ang tamang strategy sa paghahain ng mga testigo. Ngunit isinama nila iyan sa Articles of Impeachment, na ang ibig sabihin nito ay may sapat silang ebidensya para talakayin itong isyung bribery sa impeachment court,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.

(That is up to the prosecution to decide. If they believe that is the right strategy in presenting their witnesses. But they included it in the Articles of Impeachment, which means they have sufficient evidence to raise the bribery issue before the impeachment court.)
Castro, however, reminded the prosecution that dropping the bribery allegations could deprive Filipinos of the opportunity to know the full truth about the matter.

“Kung aatras sila sa akusasyong bribery laban sa Bise Presidente, hindi ba nila nasi-shortchange o nadedehado ang mga Filipino na nais sanang malaman ang buong katotohanan rito? Muli, nasa kanila po ang pagpapasya rito,” she added.

(If they withdraw the bribery allegations against the Vice President, wouldn’t they be shortchanging or disadvantaging Filipinos who want to know the full truth about the matter? Again, the decision is up to them.)

In a Super Radyo dzBB interview, House prosecution spokesperson and Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said the prosecution team was likely to drop the bribery allegations against Duterte.

“Mukhang ang direction is hindi na siya ita-tackle. Maybe that's the direction, pero hindi pa natin pina-finalize 'yan kasi ongoing pa rin ang discussion sa prosecution panel kung anong magiging susunod na hakbang pagkatapos ng Article 2,” Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.

(It appears that it will no longer be tackled. That may be the direction, but we have not finalized it yet because discussions are still ongoing among the prosecution panel on what the next steps will be after Article 2.)
Asked whether the possible decision was because the first three impeachment articles were already strong enough to convict Duterte, Adiong said this was the case.
The Senate Impeachment Court is currently hearing Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which accuses Duterte of unexplained wealth.
Article 3, meanwhile, accuses the Vice President of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her stint as DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: 'The Night of the UFOs': Remembering the Oct. 4, 1967, skies over Nova Scotia

image.caption: While Shag Harbour is considered Canada's most famous UFO incident, there were many sightings of unexplained objects in the sky over Nova Scotia on Oct. 4, 1967. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

While Oct. 4, 1967, is known for the Shag Harbour UFO incident in Nova Scotia, there were many other sightings of unexplained objects in the skies over the province that night, leading it to be known as "The Night of the UFOs."
Besides Shag Harbour, sightings were reported in Dartmouth, Sambro, Wedgeport and elsewhere
Chris Styles was just 12 years old on a clear night when he looked out his bedroom window and spotted a strange light moving along the shoreline a few blocks from his house.
He grabbed his grandfather's binoculars to get a better look and then ran out of the house, much to his dad's dismay, down to the water's edge.
"There's this huge sphere and it was a very dull orange, and it was glowing just like a poker in a fireplace," said Styles about what he saw on Oct. 4, 1967, around 10 p.m. AT.
While that date is best known for a UFO sighting in Shag Harbour in southwestern Nova Scotia, Styles was in Dartmouth, N.S.
Primarily between the Halifax area and southwestern Nova Scotia, people recorded seeing things in the sky that night, which has led ufologists to call it "The Night of the UFOs."

"If you were outside that ... night and you looked up, and for some hours afterwards, you would have seen something," said Styles. "It was a clear night. People were seeing the faintest stars without binoculars."

Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings, including Impact to Contact: The Shag Harbour Incident. He said coverage of Shag Harbour meant other sightings fell out of the press, such as what the crew of the MV Nickerson saw in the waters off Sambro.
Around 9 p.m., Capt. Leo Mersey said he spotted an object with three flashing red lights. The object, which showed up on radar, was about 25 kilometres away.

items: The man who phoned in Canada's most famous UFO sighting became the face of the mystery

blocks.text: "It was very clear that night and we could see the lights of Halifax," Mersey said in a statement he filed with the RCMP.
The radar also showed three objects about 10 kilometres away, but he could not see them.
Around 11 p.m., the object he could see went into the air, but by then had only one red flashing light.
"I had never seen anything like that before but it sounds like the thing they are looking for down off Shelburne or Barrington Passage," Mersey said in the statement, which was taken Oct. 7, 1967.
The RCMP statement, taken by a corporal with the Lunenburg detachment, noted: "Capt. Mersey is considered to be a reliable type individual and bears a good reputation in his community."
But Shag Harbour has long remained the focus, said Styles, in part because of the large witness pool, what authorities said at the time, and the subsequent paper trail left behind.
In Shag Harbour, an object with flashing lights crashed into the waters off the tiny fishing village.
Besides the many eyewitnesses, adding credence to the account was that a responding RCMP officer, Const. Ron O'Brien, described seeing a light from the object floating about 800 metres offshore.
"It was being carried out to sea by the tide and disappeared before we could get a boat to it," he told the Chronicle-Herald in an Oct. 7, 1967, article.

Styles said RCMP officers commandeered two fishing boats to see what was in the water and if there were any survivors, assuming a plane had crashed. They were joined on the boats by local fishermen and other residents.
He said depending on who you talk to, the object either disappeared or submerged, but there was a yellow foam on the water that some say smelled of sulphur.
On Friday, Oct. 6, a naval diving team was brought in, and seven divers searched through the weekend, but reported finding nothing.
The investigation reached the highest levels of National Defence.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by Col. W.W. Turner, the director of operations at National Defence headquarters, noted: "The Rescue Co-ordination Centre conducted [a] preliminary investigation and discounted the possibilities that the sighting was produced by an aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects."
His son, John Turner, told CBC News his father often mentioned to the family that he received reports of alleged UFO sightings.
"Many were easily discounted as photos of a Frisbee or a hubcap, but he often said others simply could not be explained," Turner wrote by email.

Styles wasn't the only person to see something in Dartmouth on Oct. 4, according to the Chronicle-Herald on Oct. 7, 1967. The newspaper reported that a woman on her way home from work saw a bright, round object in the sky moving from the Halifax-Dartmouth ferry terminal.
"She described it as brighter, more vivid than a star, with an orange hue like a halo around the circumference," the reporter wrote.
The woman looked at it through binoculars when she got home and saw it was not a star.

The newspaper checked with CFB Shearwater's control tower to see if anything was on the radar during the window the woman described. Control tower personnel said no one was monitoring the radar at the time.

articles.title: Lack of inspections at fish slaughterhouses a ‘disgrace’, says Animal Equality UK
articles.summary:
Charity calls for faster progress on humane slaughter laws for farmed fish in England and Wales

Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory…

blocks.text: Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed.

Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections.

When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections.

Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter. This is a huge blindspot, and it leaves these animals all the more vulnerable behind closed doors.”

In 1996, the government’s expert advisory body, the Farm Animal Welfare Council – now called the Animal Welfare Committee – suggested there should be legislation governing the slaughter of farmed fish. The committee returned to the issue in 2014 and again in 2024. On the latter occasion it urged governments across the UK to legislate for fish to be stunned before slaughter, and for inspection systems to be put in place to enforce those standards.

In its Animal Welfare Strategy for England, published in December 2025, the government committed to introducing humane slaughter requirements for farmed fish but draft legislation has yet to be published.
Penny said: “For 30 years, people in power have known that farmed fish need legal protection when they are slaughtered, yet for 30 years decisionmakers have failed to act.”

She added: “The government promised to change the law, and we welcome that promise, but promises don’t protect animals. Every month of delay leaves millions of fish at risk of prolonged, painful deaths. Ministers must bring forward species-specific slaughter legislation now, backed by a proper inspection regime, so that what happens to these animals is no longer left to chance. It’s the least they deserve.”

Animal Equality UK estimates that about 7,742 tonnes of trout a year are killed in England and Wales. The British Trout Association says the UK has almost 290 trout farms, including hatcheries, concentrated in northern England, southern England and southern Scotland.

An APHA spokesperson said: “It is incorrect to suggest fish farms aren’t regulated or inspected by government bodies. APHA investigates reports of suspected cases of poor welfare at fish farms, and the Fish Health Inspectorate inspects them on behalf of the government. We do not hesitate to take further action if we find evidence of cruelty or neglect.”

articles.title: Welsh racing ban rehoming standoff sparks fears for greyhounds’ welfare
articles.summary:
Industry says a phased end to racing, to avoid sudden jump in caring responsibilities, is unworkable

Wales’s greyhound racing ban – a UK first – has run into difficulties regarding how and…

blocks.text: Wales’s greyhound racing ban – a UK first – has run into difficulties regarding how and when to wind down the practice, potentially risking the animals’ welfare, a charity has warned.

The law, which received royal assent in April, includes a three-year window for the ban to come into effect and is overseen by a Welsh government working group, which includes racing industry representatives and animal health and welfare organisations.

Its first report, however, revealed an impasse: animal welfare groups want a phased approach to avoid caring for and rehoming hundreds of dogs in a short period of time, while industry representatives say phasing out racing is impractical.
While the Welsh government report recommended a 12-month wind-down period to support rehoming, it says it cannot mandate it, and at present there is no clear mechanism for resolving the standoff.

Claire James, the chief executive of Greyhound Rescue Wales, said: “If there is a hard stop, we and the other groups working to end greyhound racing will do whatever it takes. Our priority is making sure these animals are happy and healthy but the industry is still trying to maximise its profits.”

blocks.caption: Messua, three, at the rescue centre in Garnant.  Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena/The Guardian

blocks.text: Wales’s sole greyhound racing venue, Valley Greyhounds Stadium near Caerphilly, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Greyhound racing began in the UK 100 years ago as a working-class pursuit that made going to the races accessible for people of all incomes but the industry has been in decline for some years: most tracks now mainly rely on online betting and streaming rights rather than physical ticket sales.

Animal welfare groups say the sport is inherently dangerous: according to data from the Greyhound Board of Great Britain (GBGB), between 2018 and 2023, 2,700 greyhounds died and more than 26,500 injuries were recorded. Greyhound racing careers are short; one study calculated an average of 14 months.

The recent closure of racetracks in Oxford and Swindon has led trainers to relocate to Valley Greyhounds, meaning greyhound racing in Wales has actually increased since the ban was passed. Approximately 360 dogs and 18 trainers are currently registered at Valley Greyhounds, which the Welsh government’s implementation report said could cost up to £2,800 each to rehome.

Nicola Jones, the head of rescue and rehoming at Greyhound Rescue Wales’s site in Ammanford in Carmarthenshire, said the charity currently took in two or three dogs a week, usually through a volunteer who mediates with trainers.

blocks.caption: Nicola Jones with Messua. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena/The Guardian

blocks.text: Two dogs, Merlin and Alvin, were dropped off during the Guardian’s visit; another, Dolly, had arrived a week ago but was still too timid to come out of her kennel.

“Most of those relationships are positive, but some animals do arrive with signs of mistreatment, and many need veterinary care for fractured legs and dental disease and socialising and behaviour training after a life in kennels,” she said.

The Senedd’s decision to prohibit racing was followed a day later by a similar ban in the Scottish parliament, although the sport was already facing extinction in Scotland as the country’s last track closed in 2024. Following the Welsh and Scottish votes, at least a dozen Labour MPs, including members of the all-party parliamentary group on animal welfare, urged former prime minister Keir Starmer to bring a ban into force in England.

But potential issues with the Welsh legislation were clear early on: civil servants advised the Welsh government last year it would be better to license greyhound owners rather than bring in an outright ban on racing because “insufficient evidence” had been gathered to justify outlawing it altogether.

September’s implementation group report found that the economic impact of the ban is “yet to be quantified”. Valley Greyhound Stadium reported £15m in projected income from streaming contracts over the next five years.

The ban’s detractors also claim ministers pressed ahead as part of a deal with the Welsh Liberal Democrats to get a budget deal passed. GBGB launched a legal challenge to the bill, claiming the consultation had been rushed, but the petition was rejected by the high court.

Abbie MacGregor, the corporate affairs director at GBGB, said: “It is the people who care for these greyhounds day to day who must now manage the consequences for each dog. GBGB and its industry partners will do that work because the dogs’ welfare comes first. The Welsh government must give them the time and certainty to do it properly.”

A Welsh government spokesperson said: “This is the first in a series of reports, with further updates to follow as detailed plans continue to be developed. The implementation group will continue to refine its recommendations and provide regular progress updates to ministers.”

articles.title: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
articles.summary: Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.

image.caption: Residents of a Pompano Beach, Fla., retirement community participate in a water aerobics class. Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes as the state's governor pitches a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.

Canadians who own property in Florida describe the threats to shake them down for more money as just the latest insult in a series of them since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year with a decidedly anti-Canada agenda.

Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has railed against property taxes, which fund local governments and the services they provide — law enforcement, fire, EMS, disaster preparation and mosquito control, among many others — equating them to a form of modern-day feudalism where homeowners must "pony up money to the government just for the courtesy of using your own property."
To end this, DeSantis is pushing Amendment 3, a ballot measure crafted by his Republican statehouse allies that will be put to voters in the midterm election next month.
If passed, Florida "homesteaders," as permanent residents are called, will see a dramatic increase in an existing property tax exemption.

Any Floridian with a primary residence valued at $250,000 US or less — about 60 per cent of all homesteaders, according to the governor's office, although that figure has been questioned — would pay nothing and those with a home worth more than that would pay much less than they do now. The measure also calls on the state to eliminate homesteader property taxes entirely over time.
This constitutional amendment requires a 60 per cent supermajority, and at least one recent poll suggests it will easily clear that hurdle.
State economists project such a move will cost about $12 billion US annually, forcing local and county governments that depend on these taxes to make deep cuts, find new revenue elsewhere or both.

That's where things could get more expensive for the Canadians who own an estimated $60 billion US worth of property in the Sunshine State. DeSantis has explicitly described them as a resource to tap to close expected budget gaps.

"We need to focus on our Florida residents. And focus on, in this case, Florida homeowners, particularly our homesteaded homeowners, and we need to focus the relief there," DeSantis said at a news conference last year defending his call for lower property taxes instead of a sales tax cut.
"I want Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state and making it so Florida residents pay less taxes. I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut."

In an interview with Fox Business in June, DeSantis said that while homesteader property tax revenue will be a fraction of what it once was if the measure passes, Canadian property owners won't see any of that relief, which could help pad local coffers.
"They tax property that is non-homestead: residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial. That's a lot of money that they have," DeSantis said of local and county governments.

While reducing taxes for Floridians, the ballot measure also dictates that the assessed value of a non-homesteaded property — owned by a Canadian or another non-resident — can increase by up to 5 per cent a year, steadily raising the revenue local governments can collect.
"They are going to start getting more revenue from existing taxes without having to add new taxes and they're going to end up in a very stable situation very shortly," DeSantis said.
Snowbirds 'fed up'

DeSantis has routinely poked at Canada — including its perennially losing hockey teams. He initially mocked the trade war-induced travel boycott, saying he didn't think it would meaningfully materialize, only to see his state tourism bureau report a double-digit drop in Canadian arrivals last year.
Some Canadians who have put down seasonal roots in the state have had enough of the taunts.
Glenn McGill of Wiarton, Ont., has been wintering in North Fort Myers, Fla., a community once well-populated with fellow Canadian sunseekers, for the last 15 years.
But after Trump's second win there's been what he describes as a "stampede" of Canadians out of the park he and his wife Deb long thought of as a second home.
He says there are only four Canadians left in the sprawling retirement community, a fraction of what there once was when he first started going south.

items: Some snowbirds want out of Florida. A bad housing market makes it hard to leave

blocks.text: McGill said DeSantis's threat to lean on Canadians to make up for lost property tax revenue will only drive more of them away, including himself — he listed his home for sale.
"They're a greedy bunch of SOBs," McGill said in an interview with CBC News. "They want to drive Canadians out."
"Those who are well off really don't care but we're not rich, we're not broke, we can do the Florida thing comfortably, but starting to pay extra taxes — that would hurt," he said.
"And this political thing with Trump, I've had enough of it."
With so many Canadians leaving or staying away, McGill says the housing market in Florida has been tough to navigate as a seller.
"The market's pretty dry," he said. "It's listed, but it hasn't sold yet."
Canadians make up the vast majority of foreign property buyers in areas along Florida's Gulf Coast.
According to Realtor.com data, Canadians represent more than 70 per cent of international demand in the Cape Coral metropolitan area, which includes McGill's community.
And with Canadian sales nowhere near pre-trade war levels, the firm says local sellers face "real pricing pressure" with properties listed for weeks longer than the national average.
The areas of Florida that have historically attracted the most Canadian interest are projected to see the largest drop in home prices this year, according to the firm's projections.

Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on 3, a group opposing the property tax ballot measure, anticipates more housing market shocks given a possible flood of new Canadian-owned home listings if this tax change takes effect.
"Gosh, it wouldn't surprise me if there's an exodus of Canadians — they are going to be hit significantly," Ousley said in an interview.

"Amendment 3 is a train wreck. It's a train wreck for Floridians. It's a train wreck for those who come in the winter. Those Canadian snowbirds are going to be impacted with additional taxes — this is a tax shift, it's not tax relief," she said.
'Everyone is going to lose'
Ousley said a shrinking Canadian population base alone can't replace what will be lost if homestead taxes disappear.
Many municipalities are already warning that a sudden erosion in their tax base will decimate public services, most notably law enforcement and 911 response times.
"Everyone is going to lose with cuts," she said.
John May of Ottawa offloaded his Key West, Fla., condo after getting sick of hearing people he thought were friends parrot Trump's harsh rhetoric about Canada.
He said he felt like he was swimming in "a sea of stupidity" with falsehoods about his country commonplace.

"Trump would say something stupid, Governor Trudeau, 51st state and all that, and they'd stand there and laugh and I'd say to myself, 'Well, I just lost all respect for you,'" May said in an interview.
"And then you start avoiding people because you know what the conversation is going to be. If you try and have a logical discussion with somebody who's a Trumper, just forget about it," he said.
Jo-Ann Rowe, a Canadian who was wintering in Fort Lauderdale for years with no issue before Trump's return, had the same experience.
"The 51st state thing, my American friends all thought that was quite funny. And I really don't," she said.
She left Florida for a rental property in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. "I found it totally disrespectful. And I just couldn't do it anymore, this was my little part to do," she said.
Lilly White of Almonte, Ont., spent the last 25 years going to Tarpon Springs, Fla., near Tampa and then Flagler Beach on the other side of the state to escape Canadian winters.
White describes her time there in glowing terms, but said things changed dramatically in the Trump 2.0 era and she had to leave.

"It's not that we don't like it. We're just uncomfortable now. We'll always love the U.S. They'll always be our neighbours. They will always be friends. That's a choice we can make. But we can also choose not to fall down the rabbit hole of what's going on over there right now," she said in an interview.
"I don't like rabbit holes."
White said any move to take more property taxes from Canadians is unfair to those who have pumped a lot of money into the state's economy over the years.
The many small businesses that rely on an influx of Canadian snowbirds are surely hurting as visitor figures plummet amid the bilateral bad blood, she said.
Canadians are by the far largest single source of international tourism to the state, and the number of trips dropped by 20 per cent in the prime winter season this year, data shows.
"I can't imagine how much the businesses are losing. I know how many of my friends are not going down anymore. And we were big spenders," she said.

articles.title: Mark Carney for Nobel Peace Prize? Probably not, but his name's out there
articles.summary: If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.

image.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous Nobel Peace prize (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World·New
If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.
Carney at one point was a favourite to win on the predictions market

"[Donald] Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, told The Associated Press. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are."
Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous prize, an award Trump has made no secret he wants to win.
On Oct. 9, the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the annual Peace Prize in Oslo.

Last year, the award went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Although Trump accepted it, the Nobel Committee stressed that the prize itself remains hers.
Trump has repeatedly said he has ended eight wars, but experts say his invasion of Iran and attack on Venezuela make him an unlikely recipient this year.
Prizes in other categories will also be awarded that week, with several Canadians being discussed as possible recipients.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million US), whether awarded to an individual, small group of laureates or an organization. The deadline for nominations was Jan. 31. After months of discussions and evaluations, the committee votes in October.
Nobel Peace Prize (Oct. 9)
Earlier this week, traders on the U.S.-based prediction market Kalshi put Carney's chances of winning at 14 per cent. His odds later fell.
"I don't think his chances are great," Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CBC News.

His organization releases an annual list of potential candidates for the prize. Gjerløw said the Nobel laureate has to meet three broad criteria to win: international co-operation, disarmament and the promotion of peace.
"So it's whoever did the most for these three criteria over the past year," he said.

He said Carney's name has likely been floated because of his resistance to Trump, along with the prime minister's efforts to strengthen ties with Europe — both seen as signs of international co-operation.
But Gjerløw pointed to other possible candidates, including the International Space Station.
"It would be a symbol of what we can achieve when we are able to co-operate as humanity," he said.

Gjerløw's other candidates include Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, the Committee to Protect Journalists, and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
Nobel Prize for physiology or medicine (Oct. 5.)
When The Scientist magazine asked its readers to suggest potential Nobel Prize winners in science, Canadian researcher Dr. Daniel Drucker was among the names put forward.

The endocrinologist won a 2025 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for discovering the GLP-1 hormone used in diabetes and obesity medications — including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro — that have changed the lives of millions of people around the world.
Prediction market Kalshi has also listed Drucker as one of the top contenders to win.
Nobel Prize for Literature (Oct. 8)

Another Canadian being discussed is poet and essayist Anne Carson, who has frequently been mentioned as a strong Nobel contender. Carson is a two-time winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize, and author of Autobiography of Red, Antigonick and Red Doc>.

However, one of Canada's most famous authors, Margaret Atwood, is also a contender according to Kalshi, but at lower odds. The Handmaid's Tale author has won two Booker prizes, and for years her name has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Nobel Prize.
The last Canadian to win in this category was Alice Munro in 2013.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Canada's spy agency shakes up hiring process to 'meet operational needs': documents
articles.summary: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.

image.caption: Canada's spy agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, is working to remove 'structural bottlenecks' in its hiring process, according to documents obtained by CBC News. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.
CSIS brought in a suite of changes earlier this year to "meet operational needs and emerging demands," according to documents obtained by CBC News through an access to information request.
"These changes represent a shift in how we recruit, classify, deploy and empower our people," reads one of a series of emails sent to managers at CSIS.
"These developments and initiatives will enable us to be more efficient and effective … and better positioned to meet the demands of our changing, more challenging environment."

Most of the changes are aimed at addressing "structural bottlenecks," increasing external hires and making changes to shorten the time between recruitment and operational deployment, according to the documents.

items: CSIS may have misused power to commit offences: watchdog
Ottawa will look into screening processes amid NATO intern spying allegations

blocks.text: That includes setting up a new team dedicated to external recruitment to bring in people "efficiently and responsibly," the documents say.

As of March 2026, CSIS's hiring ratio is 85 per cent internal appointments to 15 per cent external hires, the documents show. The emails tell managers to strongly consider external talent for certain skilled positions.

Unlike other government positions, most jobs at CSIS require enhanced top secret clearance — a rigorous process diving deep into a candidate's personal background, character, family history and financial history that can take 12 to 18 months.
CSIS looking to outsource more tasks
While sections of the documents were heavily redacted, they also show a push to accelerate deployment.

Changes would see candidates apply directly to their region of choice which CSIS says would enable targeted hiring for regional vacancies. It's also bringing in adjusted official language requirements "where appropriate," and shortening training classes," according to the documents.
"It will empower us to recruit individuals who can fill critical vacancies in regions that will augment our operational capacity," reads one of the emails.
The documents show the secretive and often insular agency is looking to outsource recruitment steps including some screening, targeted recruiting and psychological assessment services.
Canadian NATO spying suspect raises questions about country’s security screening

The service has already increased its use of outsourced, standardized written testing tools to streamline the testing process. It's also restructuring how it bridges co-op students into full-time positions, it said.
CSIS is looking at acquiring new technology that "enables recruitment," but there are few details about what that could look like.

The service didn't answer questions about how many employees it needs to hire but said it's seeking to fill vacant positions for intelligence officers, engineers, analysts, IT and communications professionals "and more."
"CSIS faces growing demands due to evolving security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism," said spokesperson Magali Hébert.
"To date, CSIS has continued to have high levels of qualified applicants for its work, and recruitment efforts have garnered positive results."
Staff shortages pose risk: former analyst
Stephanie Carvin, a former CSIS analyst and now an assistant professor at Carleton University, said recruitment and retention "has for a long time been a priority concern" at the service.

"Its unique value is that it has human intelligence officers going out, speaking in the community, getting information, developing relationships, developing sources. It can't do that without people," she said.
"When you have staff shortages, you have people working overtime, they burn out, they get tired and that is a risk for the organization."
As an intelligence agency and Five Eyes partner, onboarding at CSIS is always going to be a long and "demanding" process, said Carvin, but "attempts to find efficiency are welcome."
"Someone can quit with two weeks' notice, but at the same time, it can take somewhere between a year and two years to replace them given the security requirements," she said.
"The demands on the service have probably never been greater, but at the same time, the ability to bring people in largely the same as they were in the 1980s."

A further sign the agency is worried about its staffing is its initial move to bar employees from taking the government's early retirement incentive. As CBC News reported in April, CSIS and other security agencies like the Communications Security Establishment, signalled to employees that it wouldn't accept applications citing "continued operational pressures and growth requirements."

The National Post reported that Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia then stepped in, leading to both agencies walking back their approach. According to a source who spoke to the Post, Sabia sees the early retirement offers as "a golden opportunity to breathe fresh air into the mid- to senior-levels of the public service and promote younger bureaucrats."
CSIS Director Dan Rogers, who took the reins in late 2024, has made culture change one of his top priorities.
As part of changes to the service, he brought in a new executive lead in recruitment and staffing in February, the emails shared with CBC News show.
"Welcome to the new role, I hope I didn't scare you off earlier today :)," Rogers wrote in an email.
"Given that context, you've got a very important job for the service — so glad you decided to take it on."

articles.title: The King will never live at Buckingham Palace. What does that mean for the monarchy?
articles.summary: While there have been efforts to emphasize that Buckingham Palace will continue to be the working and ceremonial headquarters of the monarchy, the recent confirmation that King Charles won’t be…

image.caption: Members from the Massed Bands of the Guards Division play on the forecourt of Buckingham Palace in London on Sept. 11. (Ben Whitley/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Hello, royal watchers and all those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your biweekly dose of royal news and analysis.

For quite a while now, it's been clear that King Charles is quite happy living at Clarence House and has little interest in moving out of that stately home and going down the road to reside in Buckingham Palace.

So it was perhaps not a huge surprise when word emerged that he would never live in that historic central London landmark — even though in ways it has become the most high-profile and visible symbol of the monarchy itself.

While there have been efforts to emphasize that the palace will continue to be the working and ceremonial headquarters of the monarchy, the confirmation that the King won't be living there could also be sending signals about the institution and its future.

"It's a real shift away from what we expect from the monarchy and … it's an example of perhaps slimming down," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.
With fewer senior members of the Royal Family, there is perhaps a move to start to "rationalize some of the properties," he said.

The shift in emphasis for the palace could also be a harbinger of a more subtle but noteworthy shift in focus for the House of Windsor as the monarchy, an institution steeped in tradition, tries to fortify its relevance in a modern world.

"The King will, in effect, use Buckingham Palace … as his office and in a sense go to work every day," said Prescott, who sees it as part of a potential distinction emerging between the institution of the monarchy and the person who holds the role of monarch at any given time, effectively becoming a custodian.

"There seems to be a shift, which perhaps is more modern thinking, because with Elizabeth II, she was the monarchy — the two were totally sort of one in the same, whereas perhaps we're teasing out a distinction between the monarchy and the monarch at any particular time."
Buckingham Palace was built in 1703 and converted into a royal palace in the 1820s.

While it had been the home of every monarch from Queen Victoria up to Elizabeth, no monarch had actually lived there since the COVID-19 pandemic. At that time, Elizabeth moved to Windsor Castle, just as a 10-year, 369-million-pound ($692 million Cdn) refurbishment project at the palace was also underway.

When Charles started his cancer treatment in 2024, there were also some advantages to the royal residence and the royal office being in separate places, Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.

"At a time when there was an enormous amount of concern about King Charles III's health and the aftermath of his cancer diagnosis, the fact that he had a short commute from Clarence House to Buckingham Palace had the effect of keeping him in the public eye without a need for formal public occasions," she said.
"Some of the symbolism that came out of that moment might also have informed this decision."
A shift in royal residences has precedents.

"There have been many periods where an established royal residence that seemed as though it would always be a royal residence — it didn't necessarily suit the needs of the next dynasty or the next generation in the Royal Family," said Harris.

"George III refused to live at Hampton Court, which had been a royal residence all the way from Henry VIII to his grandfather George II, because he didn't have good memories of that palace. He remembered his grandfather … boxing his ears there."

items: King Charles won't live in Buckingham Palace after completion of £369M renovation

blocks.text: Still, the move away from the monarch calling Buckingham Palace home feels significant.

"In the 21st century, this is being treated as a seminal moment as Buckingham Palace is so closely associated with the Royal Family today that we sometimes forget about palaces that no longer exist or mostly no longer exist, such as Whitehall or Greenwich, [which] were at one time the centre of royal power," said Harris.
With the monarch no longer living at Buckingham Palace, it remains to be seen what effect — if any — that will have on public perceptions of the monarchy.

"So many people — when they visit London, [they] visit Buckingham Palace and peer through the gates, watch the changing of the guard … always hoping they might catch a glimpse of a member of the Royal Family," said Harris.

"So it'll be interesting to see if what Buckingham Palace symbolizes transcends whether there are royalty in residence or not, or whether we see … more interest in some of the other royal residences."
Harris isn't writing off Buckingham Palace just yet.
"I think Buckingham Palace's name recognition, its appeal as a tourist destination, I think there's still going to be a lot of interest."
An 'unusual' royal phone call with Canada
As far as royal phone calls go, there don't seem to be many precedents — at least not any calls that get public attention drawn to them.
After Prince William and Prime Minister Mark Carney were on the phone together the other day, their spokespeople let it be known they'd had a chat.

The Prime Minister's Office didn't share any details of what they talked about, but a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne "discussed the enduring strength of the U.K.-Canada relationship" with Carney.
William also expressed his "longstanding affection for Canada and its people," the spokesperson said.
The call "certainly seems to be unusual," royal historian Justin Vovk said via email.
"In most situations like this, the prime minister would be speaking directly with the King as sovereign."
It's also rather unusual that the PMO would release a statement announcing that a phone call had taken place and then provide no details of what was discussed, Vovk said.

"We know that William will not speak about the conversation, so without more information, we have to assume that the PMO disclosed this conversation as an optics exercise and a reminder that Canada maintains close ties with the United Kingdom in no small part because of our shared monarchy."
The call, says Harris, shows that William's diplomatic role is expanding and he's building a "strong rapport" with political figures in the Commonwealth realms along with the United Kingdom.

Harris also noted the public reference to William's feelings toward Canada, a country he first visited as a child with his parents and younger brother, going up the CN Tower in Toronto and visiting Niagara Falls.

"Canada was the first country William and Catherine visited as a married couple and during this visit William quoted his great-grandmother Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in 1939, who stated: 'Canada made us.'"
Traditionally, Harris said via email, the heir to the throne has built relationships with Commonwealth prime ministers through royal tours and official engagements.
But there might have been another factor at play in the call between William and Carney.
"There is a personal connection between Prince William and Prime Minister Carney," Harris said.
"Prime Minister Carney's brother, Sean Carney, is chief operating officer at Kensington Palace."
Back to the U.S. and Canada

After spending several days in New York and Washington, D.C., this week, Prince Edward was in Toronto Friday, drawing to a close a North American visit that focused on areas of particular interest to the Duke of Edinburgh.

Youth opportunities and the arts were front and centre in the visit that was scheduled to take him to the Lassonde Art Trail in Toronto, along with engagements supporting the Duke of Edinburgh Awards.

Edward planned to meet with educators, award providers and students at Queen's Park Friday. The Ontario government recently announced it is investing $4 million and expanding access to the award program in schools across the province.
"Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not," Fouzia Younis, British consul general to Toronto, said in a release. "This investment into young people delivers just that: opportunity."

Earlier in the week, Edward was at the Metropolitan Opera in New York meeting representatives of the city's cultural sector. In Baltimore, he visited Western High School, the oldest all-girls public high school in the U.S., as they became a new partner school for the Duke of Edinburgh Award.
While in the Washington area, Edward also visited Mount Vernon in recognition of the 250th anniversary celebrations in the U.S. this year.
Edward's U.S. visit follows the high-profile trip there earlier this year by his elder brother, King Charles.

items: King Charles got a warm welcome from Trump, but how long will the good vibes last?
More 'soft power signals': On heels of King's visit, Prince Edward takes week-long trip to P.E.I., Ontario

blocks.text: Edward is a more frequent royal visitor — he was last in both the U.S. and Canada in 2025.
A brother's swan song for his sister

There is little doubt that Charles Spencer's recent book about his late sister Diana, Princess of Wales — published amid a mad swirl of headlines around its more incendiary claims — adds to the debate and interpretation of her legacy.

Beyond those claims — perhaps the most incendiary being that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death — the book offers new anecdotes and insights into Diana, particularly in the early years she shared with her little brother.

More broadly, Swan Song: Diana, my sister raises more questions over recent history within the upper echelons of the Royal Family, and ultimately reflects the impossibility of ever fully knowing what Diana thought or felt.

items: To read more of my review and analysis of the book, click here.
Listen to Matt Galloway's interview with Charles Spencer for CBC Radio's The Current.

blocks.text: Diana's brother doubles down on scathing King Charles allegations
Royally quotable
"I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others."
— Queen Camilla, in a speech at the Queen's Reading Room Festival at Chatsworth House.
Royal reads

King Charles plans to tour Caribbean countries beginning this month, and will "not shy away from" what he has called the "darkest days" of colonial rule and slavery, Buckingham Palace announced, but is not expected to apologize. [Guardian and ITV]

Police are investigating after two men, believed to be photographers, were seen surveilling the British school that Harry and Meghan's children attend. A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex called the incident "extraordinarily reckless." [ITV]

Charles Spencer has apologized to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book about Diana, Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s. [The Guardian]
Catherine, Princess of Wales, enjoyed a morning outdoors as she joined people recovering from drug and alcohol addictions for a gardening session for Addiction Awareness Week. [The Daily Mail]
The Prince and Princess of Wales laughed with Tom Cruise as the royal couple were greeted by the movie star at the premiere of his new film Digger in London. [The Standard]
Prince Harry fought back tears as he gave a speech on stage at a children's charity that is very close to his heart. [ITV]

articles.title: Gatchalian urges sleepyheads to watch impeachment trial at home
articles.summary: Prospective attendees who are sleep-deprived or too tired to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should watch the proceedings at home instead of sleeping inside the Senate…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:48pm

Prospective attendees who are sleep-deprived or too tired to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should watch the proceedings at home instead of sleeping inside the Senate session hall, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“If they’re sleepy, they shouldn’t come. They can sleep at home and watch the proceedings on TV because it doesn’t look good to attend the impeachment court proceedings and then sleep there. They can just watch from home if they’re feeling sleepy,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
Gatchalian made the statement after Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero called out Manila Rep. Bienvenido Abante for appearing to fall asleep during the trial.
Abante was seated in the VIP section of the Senate session hall when he fell asleep while Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña was testifying.

The House prosecution team called on the public to give Abante some leeway, saying it is normal for people of advanced age to feel sleepy at certain times of the day and that this does not make him any less of a dedicated public servant.
Senator-judge Ping Lacson also posted a photo of a sleeping Abante, saying he wondered where Abante would sleep that day, Sept. 30, after the impeachment trial was cancelled.

In a separate statement, Lacson said the prosecution had one-upped Duterte’s defense team because Abante and private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan had been caught sleeping, compared with former Chief Presidential Legal Counsel Salvador Panelo, who was on the defense side.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: PCG slams China’s obstruction of dynamite fishing probe near Pag-asa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Sunday slammed the Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) for reportedly obstructing a Philippine operation against suspected dynamite fishing by foreign…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Sunday slammed the Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) for reportedly obstructing a Philippine operation against suspected dynamite fishing by foreign vessels near Pag-asa Island.

The PCG said the agency, the Philippine Navy, and the Philippine National Police (PNP)-Maritime Group responded to reports of suspected dynamite fishing near Sandy Cays 2 and 3, about three nautical miles west of Pag-asa Island, on Sunday morning.

“At around 0720H, personnel of the Joint Task Unit Pag-asa saw a foreign fishing vessel apparently doing blast fishing in the area. CGD KIG (Coast Guard District Kalayaan Island Group) quickly formed an inter-agency team. The team deployed PCG High-Speed Response Boat HSRB-019, a Philippine Navy RHIB and rubber boat, and a PNP Maritime Group RHIB,” the PCG said.
The PCG noted that as the team left the sheltered port of Pag-asa Island around 9:50 a.m., CCG vessels 5102 and 21581 moved toward it and sounded their horns at the Philippine team.

As the team reached the fishing vessel about 500 meters east-southeast of Sandy Cay 2 around 10 a.m., the suspected small boats returned to their mother vessel. The agency said the team ordered the vessel to stop, but it ignored the orders.

As the team followed the vessel, the PCG reported that CCG 21581 blocked and shadowed the Philippine team and even came within about 10 yards of HSRB-019. The Philippine team returned safely to Pag-asa Island around 10:48 a.m. after it stopped following the mother vessel “for safety reasons.”
The PCG condemned the incident, noting that dynamite fishing is prohibited under the Philippine Fisheries Code.

“The PCG stresses that this was a routine law enforcement operation against an illegal and destructive practice. It was not directed at any country. The incident will be documented and referred through the Department of Foreign Affairs for appropriate action through existing channels,” it said.

It added that the CCG “has no law enforcement authority in the territorial sea of Pag-asa Island. By obstructing Philippine authorities, the CCG did not protect the marine environment. It made it easier for a suspected violator to escape.” /mcm

articles.title: PCG commended for vigilance vs Chinese research ship off Batanes
articles.summary: The National Maritime Council (NMC) commended on Sunday the Philippine Coast Guard"s (PCG) vigilance and continued monitoring of a Chinese research ship located within the country's exclusive…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:41pm

The National Maritime Council (NMC) commended on Sunday the Philippine Coast Guard’s (PCG) vigilance and continued monitoring of a Chinese research ship located within the country's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) off Itbayat, Batanes.
In a statement, the NMC described the Coast Guard’s response as a model of professionalism, vigilance, and restraint.

“The PCG’s response reflects an important principle of Philippine maritime governance: protecting our rights does not require unnecessary confrontation. It requires vigilance, sound judgment, professional conduct, and steadfast commitment to the rule of law,” the council said.

“... Through sustained monitoring and the deployment of BRP Teresa Magbanua (MRRV-9701), supported by maritime surveillance assets, the PCG demonstrated the Government’s resolve to protect Philippine maritime rights through coordinated, measured, and lawful action,” it added.
On September 28, the PCG reported spotting the Chinese research vessel JIA HAI KE 7 approximately 38 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, well within the Philippines’ EEZ.

PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, stated that a PCG aircraft radio-challenged the vessel multiple times, asserting the Philippines' sovereign rights while advising the ship to declare its intentions and cease any unauthorized activities.
However, the Chinese vessel did not respond to the radio challenges.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed on Friday that the Chinese research is being conducted without the consent of the Philippines, which is required under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

“Under Article 246 of UNCLOS, marine scientific research in the EEZ and on the continental shelf shall be conducted with the consent of the coastal State. The Philippines did not receive any request from the Chinese side and no consent has been given to any Chinese vessel to conduct MSR,” DFA said.

The NMC said that it remains committed to reinforcing its maritime strategy, ensuring that any developments impacting national maritime interests are handled swiftly, consistently, and with proper regard for regional stability.
The Council called on China to immediately cease its unauthorized activities within Philippine waters and adhere to international law, including UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award.

“We call on China to stop the illegal and unauthorized activities of its vessels in the Philippines’ EEZ and abide by its obligations under UNCLOS, which include the obligation to comply with the 2016 Arbitral Award that upheld the Philippines’ sovereign rights and jurisdiction over marine scientific research in its EEZ,” the NMC said. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Shadow justice secretary says despite U-turn Labour are still ‘restricting juries by the back door’, as Conservative conference begins in Birmingham

Good morning. Anthony…

blocks.text: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials

Good morning. Anthony Seldon recently published the latest in his long and invaluable series of inside stories of premierships, Sunak at 10, and he gave it the subtitle “The last Conservative prime minister?” When the book was being planned in the early days of Kemi Badenoch’s leadership of the Conservative party, it did look as though the Tories might be finished as a party of government. But now Seldon, and his co-author Tom Egerton, aren’t so sure. Their book concludes: “At the time of writing in July 2026 … the Tory party still needs to engage in a process of deep self-reflection to understand why it failed in government, and tore itself so destructively apart, if it is ever to regain power. But at this point in time we believe it is unlikely that Sunak will have been the last Tory prime minister.”

That is a victory, of sorts, for Badenoch. For most of last year there were doubts that she would still be leader by the time of the next election. But she gave a successful party conference speech, her response to the budget was much admired, and her personal approval ratings with Tory members and right-leaning voters shot up. After two years as opposition leader, Iain Duncan Smith was booted out. Two years in, Badenoch’s position as leader is safe and it is even conceivable that she could stay on if the Conservatives were to lose the next election (in part because any Tories who favour a radically different policy approach are being purged from the candidates list).

But that does not mean Badenoch’s leadership is going well. At the last election the Conservatives won 24.4% of the GB vote. According to the Politico poll of polls, they have been consistently polling below that since the end of 2024 and they are currently on 19%.

The Conservative conference starts today and, explaining her strategy in an interview in the Times, Badenoch said: “Last year was about telling the party who I was. Now the party is going to be showing the country who we are: a strong team of people who actually like each other.” The Tories have already announced quite a lot of conference-related policy.

But she has not got the news space all to herself. It is the final day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton and this morning activists are expected to debate their ‘Zionism is racism’ motion. The proposal has split the party, and critics claim that it is antisemitic. Whatever happens, it will affect how the Green party is seen.
And this morning Labour has announced a major U-turn – abandoning most of the Keir Starmer/David Lammy plans to restrict access to jury trials. Haroon Siddique has the story here.

In the past, there was an unofficial ‘gentleman’s agreement’ that the government did not make big news announcements during the opposition party’s conference. But that era (like two-party politics) is over, and Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has successfully kept Badenoch off the top of this morning’s news cycle.
Still, the Tories can claim this as a victory. This is from Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.

double quotation markThis is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour has been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the crown court.
But Timothy also claimed the U-turn did not go far enough.

double quotation markLabour are restricting juries by the back door, scrapping the right to elect one and dumping those cases on magistrates whose backlog is at a record high. Nearly 81,000 cases are stuck in the crown court, yet there is no commitment to get courts sitting more often, but Labour did find the time to write into law a review of how its reforms treat people of different backgrounds.
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, is interviewed on Sky’s Sunday with Helen Lewis.
9am: Kemi Badenoch is interviewed on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. (The interview has been pre-recorded.) Norris is being interviewed too.
Morning: The Green party debates the controversial ‘Zionism is racism’ motion on the final day of its conference this morning.

2pm: John Belsley, president of the National Conservative Convention, opens the proceedings at the Tory conference in Birmingham. The session is on the theme of “resisting separatism” and the speakers include Alex Burghart, the deputy leader and shadow Northern Ireland secretary; Mims Davies, shadow Welsh secretary; Harriet Cross, shadow Scottish secretary; Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd; and Russell Findlay, the Scottish leader.
Mid afternoon: Badenoch delivers her opening speech to the conference.
4pm: James Cleverly, who wants to be the Tory candidate for London mayor in 2028, is speaking at a fringe event.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

Bureau of Immigration

items: Authorities in Zamboanga Sibugay apprehended 244 foreign nationals in a crackdown on Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs), marking the largest operation to date in 2026.
The arrests included Chinese nationals and involved investigations into immigration violations, illegal entry, and involvement in online scams, with significant equipment seized during the raids.
This operation is part of a broader government effort to enforce the ban on POGO activities following the Anti-POGO Act of 2025

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Authorities on Friday, October 2, apprehended at least 244 foreigners in two municipalities in Zamboanga Sibugay in what the Bureau of Immigration (BI) said was the “largest” crackdown on Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) so far in 2026.
The simultaneous operations targeted suspected POGO-related activities in Barangays Kimos of Siay town, and Barangay Tandiong Muslim of Alicia town, the BI said in a statement on Sunday, October 4.

In Siay, authorities nabbed 113 foreigners, including 110 Chinese, 2 Cambodians, and 1 Hong Konger. Another 131 were apprehended in Alicia, mostly Chinese, along with Malaysians, Indonesians, and Burmese.

The BI said the identities and nationalities remain subject to verification. The raids were conducted by the BI Intelligence Division and its Mindanao units, with the National Bureau of Investigation and Armed Forces of the Philippines.

The foreigners are being investigated for alleged immigration violations, including working without the required work visa, and, in some cases, illegal entry. The BI also cited their alleged involvement in illegal POGO-related online activities.

blocks.caption: POGO. Authorities apprehend foreigners during simultaneous operations against illegal POGO activities in Zamboanga Sibugay on October 2, 2026. Photo from the Bureau of Immigration

blocks.text: In Siay, authorities also seized 78 computer monitors, laptops, cellular SIM cards, and around 3,000 mobile phones. The equipment are believed to have been used in an organized online scam operations.

The foreigners will undergo deportation proceedings for their alleged violations of Philippine immigration laws. Those issued deportation orders will be placed on the BI’s blacklist and barred from reentering the Philippines.

The operation is part of the government’s continuing crackdown on POGOs activities, which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered banned during his third State of the Nation Address in 2024. In October 2025, Marcos signed Republic Act No. 12312, or the Anti-POGO Act of 2025, which prohibits offshore gaming operations and the establishment or operation of POGO sites in the country.

But POGO operations have continued despite the ban. Authorities have carried out raids and arrests in different parts of the country in recent years, targeting suspected illegal offshore gaming operations.
BI Commissioner Joel Viado, however, said that his agency is “firmly implementing the government’s policy.”

“We will continue to enforce our immigration laws against foreign nationals who violate the conditions of their stay and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a base for illegal activities,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Constant oil price hikes enough reason to suspend fuel excise tax - Win Gatchalian
articles.summary: The continuous increase in oil prices should be sufficient reason to temporarily suspend the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 3:09pm
The continuous increase in oil prices should be sufficient reason to temporarily suspend the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“Dapat suspendihin na 'yan dahil ang gumagamit din ng diesel, gasolina ay logistics company, at ‘yan ay ipinapasa sa pagkain. Noon pa man, ang mungkahi natin ay i-suspend na rin ang gasolina, para makatulong sa pagbaba ng presyo ng mga bilihin at hindi na maipasa pa sa iba pang pangunahing bilihin,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.

(The [excise tax] should already be suspended because diesel and gasoline are also used by logistics companies, and the cost is passed on to food prices. Even before, we had already proposed suspending the excise tax on gasoline to help bring down the prices of goods and prevent the cost from being passed on to other basic commodities.)

“Dapat i-reconsider nila (economic managers) ‘yang pag suspinde rin sa excise tax sa gasolina at diesel. Dapat i-reconsider ng economic managers nation kanit temporary lang dahil umabot na ulit sa more than $80 barrel at tuloy-tuloy. Mayroon nang dahilan para suspendinin,” he added.

(The economic managers should reconsider suspending the excise tax on gasoline and diesel, even if only temporarily, because oil prices have risen above $80 a barrel again and continue to climb. There is now sufficient reason to suspend it.)
In September, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of the collection of excise tax on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and kerosene.
Marcos issued Executive Order No. 125 amid soaring global crude oil prices, which drove local petroleum prices to high levels.

According to Executive Order No. 125, "The excise taxes on LPG, except when used as raw material for production of petrochemical products or used for motive power, and kerosene, except when used as aviation fuel, are hereby fully suspended."
Marcos signed Republic Act 12316 into law in March, giving him emergency powers to suspend or reduce the excise tax rate on fuel.

Under the measure, the suspension or reduction may be implemented for up to three months if the average price of Dubai crude oil —based on the Mean of Platts Singapore (MOPS)—reaches or exceeds $80 per barrel for one month. Brent crude prices have hovered around $102 per barrel.
In a separate dzBB interview, Department of Energy Oil Industry Management Bureau Director Rino Abad said the following estimated fuel price adjustments are expected next week:

items: Gasoline - P1.50 per liter increase
Kerosene - P2 per liter increase
Diesel - P1 per liter decrease

articles.title: Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires
articles.summary:
FOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as survey highlights many fire services lack proper protective gear

The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in…

blocks.text: The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.

This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.

In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk.
However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”.

The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”.

After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late.

blocks.caption: Homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed by wildfires in August. Photograph: Alex Dodd/EPA

blocks.text: “Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel in preparing us for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Shrubsole said.

Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added.
Shrubsole said the government must agree a plan to re-wet the UK’s peat bogs, restore lost ponds in farmers’ fields, and stop grouse moor owners setting fire to moorland.

New data obtained by the Country Land and Business Association has also revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire personal protective equipment (PPE).

They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.
Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.
Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.

blocks.caption: A firefighter attempts to control a fire on moorland in the Bannau Brycheiniog, formerly known as the Brecon Beacons, in south Wales. Photograph: Jeff Morgan 03/Alamy

blocks.text: The data also revealed that training for wildfires was limited. For example, in Cleveland just five staff (1.2%) were qualified to give tactical advice or command wildfires, and in Cheshire just 8.62% of employees were trained to undertake wildfire operations.
In response to these findings, the Fire Brigades Union is calling for correct PPE to be provided to all members combating wildfires, alongside adequate training programmes.

Steve Wright, the union’s general secretary, said: “It is vital for our country’s wildfire resilience to have better land management, stronger public awareness campaigns and long-term prevention measures. Only by proper investment and a wildfire strategy can we make the country more resilient.”

A government spokesperson said: “We have made wildfire preparedness a government priority and, following incidents this summer, we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to make sure we are as resilient as possible. This includes making sure services have the right equipment and resources, building on the £100m we previously gave to upgrade our national resilience assets.

“Land management and landscape adaptation play an important part in this, and we work closely with land managers and experts to support the restoration of peatlands, the creation of firebreaks and other adaptations that help to prevent fires from starting or from spreading as quickly during incidents.”

The…

blocks.text: The government has awarded £2.3m in compensation to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) after roadworks affecting its premier garden in Wisley caused a “three-year traffic jam”.

The horticulture charity estimated it lost £13m due to disruption caused by the upgrade to the A3 and M25, with visits to the garden each year cut by 350,000. A campaign to reimburse the charity was led by the gardener and TV presenter Alan Titchmarsh.
Clare Matterson, the RHS director general, said: “I think it’s fair to say that we had three years of a traffic jam outside what is our major garden.”
Calling the compensation process “exhausting”, she added: “I would have loved more. I would have pushed for more. It is what it is, and on we go. I’m grateful that we got something.”

Matterson said the government had ignored gardening despite the fact it has proven health benefits, reducing pressure on the NHS, while the surface area of UK gardens is three times greater than all of the country’s national nature reserves combined.
However, she said she had hope for the future, not least because Andy Burnham was a frequent visitor to RHS Garden Bridgewater before he became prime minister.

blocks.caption: RHS Garden Wisley in Surrey, which saw visits drop by 350,000 during three years of roadworks. Photograph: Jubilee Images/Alamy

blocks.text: “We know he loves Bridgewater. He talked to me about going with his family, but particularly with his father to Bridgewater, and what an important place it was,” she said.
“Andy Burnham talks about pride in place and local people’s empowerment … So hopefully, Andy will think about gardening.”
The RHS runs Chelsea flower show, which came under scrutiny this year as it lost one of its biggest funders, and critics said it had gone “woke” with its focus on charities and eco-friendly gardens.

Speaking to the Guardian, Matterson issued a full-throated defence of the show for the first time. “Chelsea is our saviour,” she said. “Tickets sold out 10 days before we even opened this year. Chelsea is an extraordinary beast, and it’s become a very important sort of national moment for the country as well. It’s still watched by millions of people on the television every year.”

She added that Chelsea is “the Olympics of the horticultural world” and that it is “doing brilliantly” as the charity’s biggest fundraiser. “People, I guess, complain about anything popular, don’t they,” she said.

In the coming year, the RHS will be driving a massive push towards community gardening, getting local authorities to give pieces of unused land to residents who want to use them to grow vegetables and flowers.

“We did a survey and found about two–and-a -half – million people saying they are actively engaged in [community gardening], but something like 13 million said they would like to be, which is extraordinary,” Matterson said. “Access to land is one of the main barriers.”

blocks.caption: Clare Matterson at home in Suffolk with her dog, Minke, and a homegrown white pumpkin. Photograph: Joshua Bright/The Guardian

blocks.text: Matterson is personally involved in a community garden near her home in Suffolk. “What I love about that is that not everybody that comes loves the physical act of gardening,” she said. “Some like making things, and so they’ll be making bird boxes. Some people just want to come and chat.”

She hopes Burnham’s push towards pride in local places will start a community gardening revolution. “Community gardening must be a big thing for this country,” she said. “It’s about health, wellbeing and the opportunity for localities to make a big difference for their communities. If we can take that seriously, it’s not a big investment across the country, but I think the benefits that flow out from it are absolutely enormous.”
Another project she is helming aims to get gardens into NHS hospitals to provide peace and respite for patients, their families and staff.

“The hospitals that have got those gardens are seeing higher retention rates among their staff, better morale and wellbeing,” she said. “For someone visiting a relative who’s really unwell, being able to go and sit in the garden makes a huge difference.”

With gardening societies such as the RHS having a historical reputation as elitist, Matterson says she is trying to make the RHS as inclusive as possible. The charity is hosting an urban show in Bristol next year, focused on pot plants, small spaces and balcony gardens.

“Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” she asked. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody? That was the conversation we had across the organisation. Our strategy now is: how do we get horticulture to as many people as possible?”
