articles.title: Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo brings Filipino flavor to space science
articles.summary: ‘There's actually a huge history of indigenous Filipinos doing astronomy, and we just don't talk about it,’ says Fil-Am astrophysicist Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo

blocks.text: Ever heard someone explain the formation of black holes by comparing it to the classic Filipino sinigang recipe?
This is something only Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo could pull off. Almost instantly, the Filipino-American astrophysicist caught the attention of her listeners during a talk on astronomy in Manila.
For someone who grew up in the US, Berger-Marcelo still makes sure that her teachings reflect her Filipino roots.

“My mom was born in Palawan and immigrated when she was in her teens. Growing up, I was confused about my background,” Berger-Marcelo shared. “My mom had a lot of trauma here as a child — that was one of the reasons why she left, so she’s never wanted to come back. Not because of the Philippines, but because of her family life here. It was really hard to connect to my culture.”

“My family on my dad’s side is just my grandma, so I basically just grew up with my Filipino family. I think, actually, it’s helped me in astrophysics because I just learned this word: kapwa. My grandma and my mom know how to build community.”
At 30 years old, Berger-Marcelo visited the Philippines for the first time, accompanied by her 84-year-old grandmother, whom she’s very close with.

“Growing up in the US, there were a lot of opportunities to get involved and do research. That’s one of the reasons why I wanted to come to Manila: to meet Filipino astrophysicists, help diversify astronomy, and find out what people are doing here,” she said.

Berger-Marcelo is a PhD candidate in physics at the University of Melbourne, Australia. Her interests in astronomy, astrophysics, instrumentation, cosmology, and other branches of science have led her to various paths, including indigenous Filipino astronomy.

“There’s actually a huge history of indigenous Filipinos doing astronomy, and we just don’t talk about it. It’s in your blood,” she said. “In Australia, there are big programs dedicated to indigenous Australian astronomy, so it’s slowly evolving.”

Berger-Marcelo graduated with a bachelor’s degree in astrophysics at UC Berkeley in 2018, then took her masters in physics at McGill University in 2022, before becoming a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne.
In 2019, she worked as a data science intern at NASA Ames, a major research center of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in California, then later took some time off to travel.
Like many Filipinos, Berger-Marcelo also loves singing.

“I actually grew up wanting to be a musician. I loved singing. I wanted to be like Olivia Rodrigo. In college, they made me choose between music and astronomy, and so I said, ‘Okay, I’ll do astronomy instead,’ because I always knew I was interested in it,” she shared.

“I love it because the problems that I get to work on, I feel like, are some of the most interesting ever. They’re so cool. I just gave a talk on black holes; it doesn’t affect anything we do on Earth, but it’s still really interesting.”
During her talk in Manila, Berger-Marcelo shared why she enjoys teaching.

“In astrophysics, it tends to be very individual — everyone for themselves, a very self-absorbed, narcissistic field,” she said. “I think that’s been one of the greatest things I’ve learned from being Filipino: connecting with people and trying to do it as a group rather than just being on my own. I want to bring other people up with me.”
Berger-Marcelo was a lecturer at the Hackbright Academy and also conducted workshops and private tutoring. So it’s no surprise that she wanted to do the same in her mother’s home province.
“That’s one of the things I want to do in Palawan, at Palawan State University. There’s no astrophysics program in Palawan,” she said.
But then, Berger-Marcelo understands the many gut issues Filipinos have to face.

“Coming here, I think, ‘wow, how can I be studying astrophysics when there are all these people that can barely get to work because of flooding?’ There are so many major political issues and poverty,” she said. “It’s really hard to reconcile, and I don’t think I have an answer for it yet.”
Still, Berger-Marcelo noted the importance of pursuing science.
“Everyone should have the opportunity, but simultaneously, we need to work on ways to do astrophysics while also addressing problems like climate change or poverty in the Philippines,” she said.
“First, you need to make sure that kids can get to school and have enough food to study. Kids need to be emotionally and physically healthy to then be able to study.”
“There’s so much potential, there are so many amazing astrophysics students [here],” she added. “They deserve to have access to astronomy just like the rest of the world.”
For now, Berger-Marcelo hopes to continue using her voice and knowledge to inspire future scientists.

“I’m really proud of my mentorship and how I’ve given back to science through science communication and mentoring,” she said. “I care a lot about that — that’s the whole reason I’m here.” – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: JV Ejercito bill seeks to double indigent seniors' pension to P2,000
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito has filed a bill seeking to double the monthly social pension for indigent senior citizens from P1,000 to P2,000 amid rising prices of goods and other basic needs.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 2:57pm
Senator JV Ejercito has filed a bill seeking to double the monthly social pension for indigent senior citizens from P1,000 to P2,000 amid rising prices of goods and other basic needs.
Senate Bill No. 2522 seeks to amend Republic Act No. 11916, which doubled the monthly social pension from P500 to the current P1,000.
Ejercito said the P1,000 monthly pension is no longer enough to cover the needs and expenses of senior citizens.

“Seniors should not be forced to choose between buying medicine and buying food. Their lifetime of work and sacrifices should not end in anxiety over whether there will be enough money for the next meal or the next prescription,” Ejercito said in the bill’s explanatory note.
“Social pension is not charity. Ultimately, this measure is about how we value those who came before us,” he added.

The proposed measure would expand the definition of an indigent senior citizen to include those with no regular income or pension, as well as retirees receiving pensions or financial assistance of P10,000 or less per month, as determined by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
The bill would also remove the existing requirement that an indigent senior citizen be frail, sickly or disabled to qualify for the pension.

Moreover, the bill would require the DSWD, with the approval of the Department of Budget and Management and after consulting stakeholders, to review and adjust the social pension amount every two years based on economic indicators such as the consumer price index and cost of living.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Impeachment court may rule on Sara Duterte case by end-November --Sen. Gatchalian
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court is targeting to issue its ruling on Vice President Sara Duterte"s case by the end of November, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 2:26pm
The Senate impeachment court is targeting to issue its ruling on Vice President Sara Duterte’s case by the end of November, Senate President and senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.

“Ako personally, baka we need mga 30 to 45 days from now... Ang isyu lang, magkakaroon kami ng 2-week break sa end of October. Hopefully within 30 to 45 days (calendar days),” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
(I personally think we may need 30 to 45 days from now. The only issue is that we will have a two-week break at the end of October. Hopefully, within 30 to 45 calendar days.)
“Siguro mga mid-November to end of November [posibleng matapos ang impeachment trial at makapaghatol kay VP Duterte]. Tingin ko,” he added.
(Maybe by mid-November to the end of November, the impeachment trial could be completed, and a verdict could be handed down on VP Duterte.)
Gatchalian further said the goal is to finish the impeachment proceedings before Christmas, but recent changes may allow them to wrap up sooner.
“Marami kasing pagbabago. Una sa lahat, bumilis... Pangalawa, maraming testigo ang tinanggal at nagbigay ng mas mahabang oras ang impeachment court,” he said.
(There have been many changes. First, the proceedings have moved faster. Second, several witnesses were dropped, and the impeachment court gave us more time.)
The Senate impeachment court is currently tackling Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on the unexplained wealth of Duterte.
In a separate dzBB interview, House trial spokesperson Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said the prosecution team is considering dropping the bribery charges against Duterte.

"Mukhang ang direction is hindi na siya ita-tackle. Maybe that's the direction pero hindi pa natin pina-finalize 'yan kasi ongoing pa rin ang discussion sa prosecution panel kung anong magiging susunod na hakbang pagkatapos ng Article 2," Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.

(It appears that it will no longer be tackled. That may be the direction, but we have not finalized it yet because discussions are still ongoing among the prosecution panel on what the next steps will be after Article 2.)
Adiong then confirmed when asked whether the decision was because the first three impeachment articles were already strong enough to convict Duterte.
Article 3 accuses the Vice President of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her stint as DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
articles.summary: State police and the country's security agency are looking into the co-pilot, who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel.

blocks.text: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.
The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.
The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.
The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.
In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".
The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".

Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel.
Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar, and Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.
He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

articles.title: Filipino shoppers ranked as Southeast Asia's 'savviest' online
articles.summary: Report says 36% qualify as savvy, with monthly spending 47% higher.

blocks.text: The Philippines posted the highest savvy-shopper share among six Southeast Asian markets, according to a Lazada-Cube report.
Nic Law via Pexels
MANILA, Philippines — Filipino online shoppers emerged as Southeast Asia's "savviest" consumers in a 2026 regional e-commerce report, with more than one in three falling into its top shopper segment.
The 2026 eCommerce Savvy Shopper Report for the Philippines found that 36% of Filipino shoppers qualified as "savvy," the highest share among six Southeast Asian markets covered.
Another 22% were classified as "near-savvy," bringing the combined share to 58%, also the largest pool in the region.
The Philippines was followed by Indonesia, where 28% of shoppers were classified as savvy, Vietnam at 25%, Thailand at 22%, Malaysia at 20% and Singapore at 9%.
Filipino savvy shoppers also stood out for how much more they spent.
Their monthly spending was 47% higher than that of general shoppers, the biggest difference among the six markets.
Vietnam followed with a 44% spending uplift, Malaysia with 36%, Thailand with 27%, Indonesia with 19% and Singapore with 13%.

The report estimated the weighted spending gap associated with savvy shoppers in the Philippines at $3.3 billion in 2026. It said the estimate was based on annual e-commerce marketplace spending in Southeast Asia in 2026.
What makes a shopper 'savvy'?

The report, jointly conducted by e-commerce company Lazada and market data firm Cube, assessed shopper savviness across four dimensions: verification, value optimization, digital fluency, and confidence and protection.
These measured whether consumers choose the right products, get the best value, use available digital tools effectively and feel protected when something goes wrong with a purchase.
Across Southeast Asia, the report found that shoppers were more willing to put in additional effort to secure better value than give up trust-related protections.
Forty-three percent said they were willing to wait longer for delivery, 41% would spend more effort finding a deal and 36% would compare offers.
By comparison, only 14% were willing to give up authenticity signals, while 13% would sacrifice purchase protection.
The Philippines also stood out as the only Southeast Asian market in the report where Gen X and Gen Z shoppers were equally willing to pay more for stronger purchase protection.
The report described this as an indication that trust cuts across generations rather than being limited to younger online consumers.

The Philippines report, however, did not disclose key survey methodology, including its sample size, sampling and recruitment method, fieldwork period or the scoring thresholds used to classify shoppers as "savvy" or "near-savvy."

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] Building safe online spaces requires whole-of-society approach
articles.summary: The Safe Online Spaces forum tackles different aspects of online safety, from legal and technological issues to community and family-related efforts, to foster safe spaces for children

blocks.text: The Safe Online Spaces forum tackles different aspects of online safety, from legal and technological issues to community and family-related efforts, to foster safe spaces for children

items: The Safe Online Spaces forum brought together various stakeholders, including telecommunications companies, law enforcement, and mental health professionals, to discuss strategies for ensuring online safety for children amidst rising concerns about digital threats.

Three panel discussions focused on defining regulations for online safety, addressing harmful content, and strengthening community support for children's digital resilience, emphasizing the need for parental involvement and awareness.
Meanwhile, PLDT's COO highlighted the importance of collaboration among different sectors to tackle online safety challenges, acknowledging that no single entity can solve the problem alone,

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

At a PLDT and Smart event dedicated toward starting the conversation on building safer online spaces for children, I saw members of the community at large discuss ways on how they could foster safety in the digital age, especially given reports of school shootings and the spread of child sexual abuse material.

The Safe Online Spaces forum, held Tuesday, September 29, convened telecommunications companies, law enforcement agencies, mental health professionals, parents and other stakeholders. They held three panel discussions on different aspects of online safety, from legal and technological issues to community and family-related efforts, to help bring about these safe spaces for kids and teens.

As a member of the media who did not have a child, I felt out of place during the proceedings, but as the day went on, I felt like everyone had a part to play in fostering a safe environment for the young.

PLDT chief operating officer and chief technology officer Menardo Jimenez said during the forum’s opening speech that the problem of keeping and maintaining safe online spaces for the young was one “that can’t be solved by telcos or government playing God.”

blocks.caption: MENARDO JIMENEZ. PLDT chief operating officer and chief technology officer Menardo Jimenez speaks at the Safe Online Spaces forum on September 29, 2026.

blocks.text: JImenez added that such a task “will be solved by the sectors in this room talking with each other, understanding what the problem is, and coming up with a solution to solve this problem together.”
There were three panel discussions around specific themes.
The first panel tried to define the safeguards by explaining existing regulations and policies or basically, what can and can’t be done in the process of protecting children online.

During this panel, lawyer Jaye dela Cruz-Bekema, chief legislative staff officer for the Office of Senator Risa Hontiveros brought up the Batang Ligtas Act — formerly Senate Bill No. 1819 or the Sagip Bata Act — which the Senate ratified recently.
Word of the impending ratification at that time was met with applause, and it was nice seeing political will being celebrated and enacted in this way.

blocks.caption: Safe Online Spaces forum, PLDT smart

blocks.text: The second panel featured Bea Bautista, TikTok’s communications lead for the Philippines, Malaysia, and Thailand; national esports athlete and Philippine Tekken champion Alexandre “AK” Laverez; AK’s father, lawyer Ronie Laverez; and tech journalist Jayvee Fernandez,

During this panel, they shared their views on how to identify and address harmful content, prevent the amplification of such content, and deal with possible online threats. This included reminding people that tech companies, both for the devices being used and the apps on said devices, had built-in features to address parental concerns.

These, however, required an investment of attention and time from parents, who may not be as tech-savvy as their kids. One of the potential problem points in creating safe spaces online is that sometimes, parents or other adults don’t know how to navigate the online world as deftly as their children.

blocks.caption: Preventing school violence starts at home, but gov’t must step up

blocks.text: To that end, the final panel discussion dealt with how specific societal units — families, schools, and the communities at large — can strengthen children’s digital resilience and provide support when online threats or harms occur.

blocks.caption: Safe Online Spaces forum, PLDT, Smart

blocks.text: In this discussion, it was commonly brought up that parents needed to step up, so to speak, to be there for their kids, even if they don’t have the tech skills required to police kids’ gadgets 24/7.

This panel brought out strategies for parents, teachers, and other community members to allow them to become the safe spaces kids need in times of crisis. It was touching, even though it also felt like it was meant for those privileged enough to be available for children to seek out.

This is something I felt was left not entirely addressed, as not all parents can be there for their kids, especially if they’re OFWs separated by distance. But there may be other times for people to tackle that topic on. Only so much can be done in four hours.

blocks.caption: [DECODED] Child safety isn’t a parenting problem. It’s a platform failure.

blocks.text: The Safe Online Spaces forum last Tuesday aims to be the first of many such events, allowing different stakeholders to share ideas and ask questions of the community on promoting online safety for children and teens.

Jimenez, during his opening speech, acknowledged that there were limitations to what a telecommunications company could do, and simply reacting to online threats will not solve the issue of online harm; the issue will also not be solved by any one company alone.

He added, “Our role as PLDT is to use our network and our reach to help reduce these digital risks, and to gather different perspectives to come up with clear priorities and practical recommendations as we move forward.”

As a member of the media, I suppose I also have a part to play: that of sharing what threats are out there, and what a whole-of-society approach can do to build better online spaces for everyone. – Rappler.com

articles.title: OpenAI safety employee quits, says ‘time for trial and error is over’
articles.summary: David Robinson warns that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment

blocks.text: OPENAI. A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed OpenAI logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
David Robinson warns that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment
A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company’s approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures.

Writing in “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” published by the Atlantic on Saturday, October 3, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being “nearly careful enough” and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems.
“The time for trial and error is over,” Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation.
Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge.

The comments add to a debate within the AI industry over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly.

Robinson, who said he spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, helped draft the company’s preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.

Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers’ understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.summary:
‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access

They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent

blocks.text: They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.

blocks.caption: The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March last year by the Abortion Dream Team. Photograph: Martyna Adamska

blocks.text: Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind this week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”

The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.

Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.

While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.

blocks.caption: Protests against the tightening of abortion laws, Oct 2020 in Warsaw. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty Images

blocks.text: The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”

The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
after newsletter promotion

Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”

But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”

While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.

It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

articles.title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
articles.summary:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China…

blocks.text: Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.

EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.

Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.

“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.

“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.

Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.

The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion

Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”

Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”

He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title: 3 Japanese scholars examine Filipino migration story in UAE
articles.summary: Japanese professors specializing in Philippine studies launch a pioneering book that documents the history and daily lives of OFWs in the United Arab Emirates

items: Three Japanese professors, Drs. Naomi Hosoda, Masako Ishii, and Akiko Watanabe, are launching a book on overseas Filipino workers in the UAE to document their lives and the impact of Filipino migration over the past 50 years.

The book, titled 'Filipino Migration to the United Arab Emirates: Trajectories of Navigating Long-term Temporariness,' includes contributions from seven authors and covers various aspects of Filipino migration, entrepreneurship, and the socio-economic ties between Japan and the Philippines.

The authors emphasize the need for more literature focusing on the Filipino community in the Gulf, as existing studies primarily cover other expatriate groups, and they aim to raise awareness about the challenges faced by Filipino migrants.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Why would three college professors from Japan write a book on overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in UAE?

Drs. Naomi Hosoda, Masako Ishii, and Akiko Watanabe said they’ve always been interested to study the Philippines — to learn more about its people, and perhaps, provide the world a better understanding of the Filipinos.

Hosoda, who has been in the Philippines for seven years — four in Manila where she worked as a journalist for the Manila Shimbun from 1994 to 1998, and some more years in Samar where she, then a doctorate student, conducted ethnographic research on the Samarnon migration — has long been curious to learn about the Filipino movement elsewhere around the world.

“My interest in the Philippines began when I was a graduate student in Canada and chose the country as the focus of my research topic. Why do so many Filipinos go abroad to work in such a wide range of professions?“ she asked.

blocks.caption: Dr. Akiko Watanabe (third from left) at an elementary school in Bicol. Contributed photo

blocks.text: Ishii, who, from March 1995 to March 1996 was based in General Santos City and Sarangani Province, has, since 2022, spent more than a year in total in Cotabato City monitoring the transition process of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Watanabe, meanwhile, has stayed mostly in Manila from 2001 to 2006, and traveled to different places in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

All holding doctorates and specializing in Philippine studies, the three Japanese scholars are set to launch a book about Filipino migration to the UAE. Alongside seven contributing authors, the book explores why the country has become one of the top destinations for OFWs.

They decided to write the book to document how the lives of Filipinos in the Gulf have transformed over the years. They noted that it has been over 50 years since the Philippines first began exporting labor to alleviate economic stagnation at home and meet the growing demand for workers in the Middle East during the 1970s oil boom.
“Gulf cities like Dubai have experienced drastic changes since the 1970s. But what about the people living there?” Hosoda asked.
The professors highlighted that while existing literature covers the daily lives of Indian, Arab, and European expatriates in the Gulf, no books have focused specifically on the Filipino community.

“We chose the UAE as our case study site because it is where we conducted most of our research, and it is widely seen as a model country for urban development driven by a global workforce,” Hosoda said.

“The nexus of the Philippines as the sending country and the UAE as the receiving county, we imagined, could be a very interesting case study for us to learn how a massive human flow could transform both urban spaces and migrant people.”
Filipinos comprise the fifth biggest number of foreigners in the UAE at one million, according to official estimates.
“We also need to emphasize the fact that we were able to conduct research in the UAE because of the kindness of people we encountered there, especially Filipinos living in the country,” Hosoda said.
The book, entitled Filipino Migration to the United Arab Emirates: Trajectories of Navigating Long-term Temporariness, also features seven contributors — five Filipinos and two French.
It has 12 chapters discussing subjects from origins of the migration to the UAE, to Filipino entrepreneurship and what lies ahead, among others. Work on the book started in 2024.
The three scholars are no strangers to the contemporary Philippine setup.

“I had been studying about Muslims in Manila and then explored my focus on Filipinos in the Gulf. It’s partly to return the favor for all the kindness they’ve extended to me, and partly because I want to further raise/change their standing in Japan and around the world,” said Watanabe.
Ishii also finds it interesting to note the economic relations between Japan and southern Philippines, and the armed conflict there.

“Mindanao is an island from which Japan has long imported timber, bananas, pineapples, and tuna. Japan and the southern Philippines have therefore long maintained significant historical and economic ties,” she said.

“Nevertheless, the armed conflicts that have taken place in this neighboring country remain relatively little known among the Japanese public. This is one of the reasons why I have continued to study and teach about the southern Philippines.”
Ishii first learned more about the country in 1989, during which she found out about the war in the southern Philippines.
“Since then, I have become interested in studying the armed conflicts in a country neighboring Japan,” she said.

“I have also learned that the armed conflict and the resulting displacement had expanded the physical range of movement of Muslim women. Some eventually began traveling abroad to work as overseas Filipino workers. However, many of them experienced mistreatment while working in the Middle East,” Ishii added.
“This, in turn, compelled me to document the experiences of Muslim Filipina domestic workers and to draw attention to the challenges they faced.”
Hosoda, meanwhile, has been keen to pass on what she has learned to her students.

“After finishing my master degree, I became a journalist and then a doctoral student in Japan. Finally, I became a researcher, and write books and papers. Basically, I have been researching the same topic ever since,” she said.

“I teach my students in Japan and elsewhere what I have learned from my research because the lives of the Filipino migrants I have encountered teach us many important life lessons, such as values, faith, community, nation, and history.”
What’s even more interesting is why their students are taking up Filipinology.
“They are interested in the Philippines as a country where people speak English, and they view it as a country struggling with poverty,” said Watanabe.
Intercultural marriages is another factor.
“Students at my college are interested in Filipinos, as many of them have had classmates of Filipino descent — whose mother or father is Filipino — since elementary or high school,” said Ishii.
Migration is another interest in Hosoda’s classes at Nagasaki University.
“I teach about Filipino society and their out-migration to approximately 100 undergraduate students and several graduate students per year,” noted Hosoda.
“Undergraduate students take my courses because they are interested in learning about Asian countries other than Japan and/or the actual lives of international migrants, including Filipinos.”

Watanabe is an associate professor at the Bunkyo University’s Faculty of International Studies in Tokyo. She has a doctorate from Kyoto University awarded in July 2012. Her thesis is about the formation of Muslim communities in Metro Manila.

Ishii is a professor at Rikkyo University’s College of Intercultural Communication also in Tokyo. She has a doctorate in international relations awarded in 2000 in Sophia University, likewise in Tokyo. Her thesis is Stories of Muslim Women in the Philippines: Armed Conflict, Development, and Social Change.

A professor in Nagasaki University’s School of Global Social Sciences and Humanities, Hosoda has a doctorate degree in Southeast Asia Area Studies from Graduate School of Asian and African Area Studies in Kyoto University. Her thesis was entitled, Socio-cultural Aspects of Migration from Samar Island, Philippines. The doctorate was awarded in 2007. She also has two awards for her previous book, Searching for ‘Luck’: An Ethnography of Filipino Migrants and their Affective Ties.
The three have written other books about migration into the Gulf. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Prosecution likely to drop bribery charges in VP Sara Duterte impeachment --Adiong
articles.summary: The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is likely to drop the bribery charges against her, House prosecution spokesperson Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 12:59pm

The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is likely to drop the bribery charges against her, House prosecution spokesperson and Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Alonto Adiong said Sunday.

"Mukhang ang direction is hindi na siya ita-tackle. Maybe that's the direction pero hindi pa natin pina-finalize 'yan kasi ongoing pa rin ang discussion sa prosecution panel kung anong magiging susunod na hakbang pagkatapos ng Article 2," Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.

(It appears that it will no longer be tackled. That may be the direction, but we have not finalized it yet because discussions are still ongoing among the prosecution panel on what the next steps will be after Article 2.)
When asked whether the decision was because the first three impeachment articles were already strong enough to convict Duterte, Adiong confirmed.
"That's one way of looking at it kasi bakit mo pa papahabain 'yung trial kung para sa amin naman ay napakita namin 'yung mga kinakailangan na ebidensiya," Adiong said.
(That is one way of looking at it because why prolong the trial if, in our view, we have already presented the necessary evidence.)

"Kasi unang-una, hindi lang role ng prosecution... hindi lang to make sure may trial o may pagkakataong magpresenta ng ebidensiya. Ultimately, ang sini-seek natin dito is justice, justice para sa taongbayan," he added.

(Because, first and foremost, the role of the prosecution is not merely to ensure that there is a trial or an opportunity to present evidence. Ultimately, what we are seeking here is justice for the Filipinos.)
The Senate Impeachment Court is currently tackling Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on unexplained wealth of Duterte.
Meanwhile, Article 3 accuses the Vice President of bribing officials of the Department of Education during her stint as DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Polls suggest the election will be a closely run contest between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing rival.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
The two candidates leading in the polls are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro
ByVanessa Buschschlüter
Latin America online editor
Brazilians are voting on Sunday in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names.
The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, will be challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro.

In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Here's what you need to know.
The man not on the ballot

blocks.caption: Image caption, At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacy

blocks.text: Image source, Nelson ALMEIDA / AFP via Getty Images
At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacy
Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election.
Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election.
At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.

When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.
What do the polls say?
While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.
BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.
The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less.
If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October.
The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out.
BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all.
Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot.

Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.
What does Lula stand for?

blocks.caption: Image caption, In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereignty

blocks.text: Image source, Olga Fedorova/EPA/Shutterstock
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereignty
Lula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already.

He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família.
The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.
Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.
When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month.

There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls.
What is Bolsonaro promising?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supporters

blocks.text: Image source, Adriano Machado/Reuters
Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supporters
Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019.

The younger Bolsonaro is running for the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) and, while he is widely seen as less confrontational than his father, he is appealing to the followers of the older Bolsonaro by promising to broadly continue in his footsteps.

During his time in the Senate, the trained lawyer has advocated a tough-on-crime stance, calling for longer sentences and laxer gun laws, arguing that "decent citizens" should be able to defend themselves from criminals.

He has successfully lobbied for the US to declare Brazil-based criminal gangs Comando Vermelho (CV) and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a move that was opposed by Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro has also courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry as part of his campaign.
He has said that he will cut what he says are unnecessary regulations and "get the state off farmers' backs".

Quizzed in an interview with Globo in August on whether he still believed - as he had said in 2019 - that climate change did not exist, he acknowledged that there had been "extreme climate events", but insisted that these events were "cyclical".
Flávio Bolsonaro has actively courted Trump and members of his administration by portraying himself as a loyal ally during a meeting at the White House in May.
More recently, he promised to join the US-led anti-crime alliance that the Trump administration has dubbed "Shield of the Americas", should he be elected.
What are the main issues worrying voters?
Up until a few months ago, Brazilians told pollsters that crime and security were their main concerns.
But in the weeks leading up to the election, a scandal involving a jailed banker accused of orchestrating one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases has pushed corruption to the top of the list.
The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, is well connected and has ties to many powerful people in Brazil - both on the political right and left.
Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).
Police have since then opened an investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for suspected corruption and money laundering over the financing of the film.
But pollsters say Lula's campaign was also hurt by the Vorcaro scandal, after alleged links emerged between the disgraced banker and an ally of Lula, the Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Moraes is the man who presided over Jair Bolsonaro's trial and has made a number of subsequent rulings about the conditions of his detention.
A police report suggested that Vorcaro had made numerous calls and sent a number of messages to a phone number which officers say is linked to Moraes.
The investigators say Vorcaro asked the person with whom he was communicating for help avoiding arrest.

Moraes has denied any wrongdoing but these latest revelations mean that, in the crucial weeks before the election, attention shifted away from the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro to those against the Supreme Court justice.
Lula has tried to distance himself from Moraes, saying that "no one is above the law", but his rival has already pounced on the allegations against the judge to make political hay.
"Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes," Flávio Bolsonaro told his supporters at a rally, using the right's intense dislike of the judge to shore up his own support.

articles.title: COA: P10.39-B in terminated solar contract obligations tied to Leviste-linked firms
articles.summary: Leviste-linked firms account for P10.39 billion of flagged solar obligations

blocks.text: October 4, 2026 | 12:44pm
MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged the Department of Energy (DOE) over P10.77 billion in outstanding financial obligations from 37 terminated solar energy contracts.
In its audit report on the DOE for calendar year 2025, the agency cited 96% of contracts are attributed to companies under Solar Philippines group founded by Rep. Leandro Leviste (Batangas).
Auditors warned of a risk that the government may fail to collect the financial obligations arising from the terminated Solar Energy Operating Contractsm or SEOCs.
The obligations cover unfulfilled work program and training commitments, development assistance and contractual penalties.
Of the P10.77 billion demanded from developers, P10,389,331,719.44 was attributed to companies under the Solar Philippines group.

State auditors noted that the P10.39-billion amount is equivalent to about 494 years of the annual funding requirement of the DOE's Solar Energy Management Division, which had a P21.02-million allotment for 2025.

"This comparison highlights the significance of the outstanding obligations and underscores the importance of adopting timely and effective measures to ensure their collection in order to protect government interest," COA said.
Contracts terminated over noncompliance
Most of the contracts were terminated over developers' failure to comply with approved work programs, renew required performance bonds or meet material terms and conditions, according to the audit.

Some contracts were terminated "due to the developers' non-compliance with the approved Work Program, non-renewal of the required performance bond, and failure to comply with the material terms and conditions of the contracts," COA said.
A number of contracts were also ended after developers voluntarily surrendered them.

Among the contracts identified in the audit was the Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 Solar Power Project under Solar Philippines Nueva Ecija Corp., which carried more than P10.34 billion in financial obligations.

COA urged the DOE to exhaust legal and administrative remedies to collect the outstanding amounts, strengthen its monitoring of active contracts and review its policies on awarding and implementing solar energy service contracts. Such steps, it said, should reduce cancellations and the resulting loss of potential generating capacity.
DOE seeks legal action

In response to the audit findings, the DOE said its Legal Division for Renewable Energy had referred the Solar Philippines service contracts to the Office of the Solicitor General for appropriate legal action.
The department is pursuing about P24 billion in financial obligations and penalties from Solar Philippines-linked companies, covering contracts terminated in 2024 and 2025.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin earlier said 33 terminated contracts linked to the group represented more than 11,400 megawatts of committed renewable energy capacity.
The agency also said remedies involving 36 other solar developers with terminated contracts are being considered.
Impact on power supply
For the auditing agency, terminated contracts reduced the renewable energy capacity that the projects had been expected to contribute to the country's power supply.
The audit report described the cancellations as resulting in "approximately 6.796 Gigawatts-hours of unrealized potential generating capacity."

"Such foregone capacity represents a substantial diminution in the anticipated expansion of solar energy resources, which could have supported the government's objective of enhancing energy security, diversifying the power generation mix, and increasing the share of renewable energy in the national energy supply," COA said.

The audit findings come as the Office of the Ombudsman conducts a preliminary investigation into plunder and graft complaints against Leviste, his mother Sen. Loren Legarda and former Alfonso Cusi, a former energy secretary, over separate allegations involving solar energy projects.
The respondents have denied wrongdoing.

Legarda and Leviste have submitted counter-affidavits to the Ombudsman. Legarda is currently undergoing medical treatment in France and has extended her Senate medical leave through October 9, while her spokesperson said Leviste is with her to assist with her medical needs.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The road to plenty: Four titans and the battle for the Santa Rosa peso
articles.summary: Four of the country’s most powerful corporate dynasties—Ayala, SM, Villar, and Gokongwei—are converging on a single corridor to fight over household wallets in a growth area in Laguna

blocks.text: Four of the country’s most powerful corporate dynasties—Ayala, SM, Villar, and Gokongwei—are converging on a single corridor to fight over household wallets in a growth area in Laguna

items: Thirty years ago, Santa Rosa was a remote area with poor infrastructure and limited shopping options, but it has now transformed into a competitive retail hub in Southern Luzon.
Major retail players like SM Prime Holdings and Ayala Malls are expanding aggressively in the area, leading to a clash of corporate strategies as they vie for consumer spending.
The shift in retail dynamics reflects broader suburban growth and decentralization, with local families now having a significant influence on the success of these corporate giants.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Thirty years ago, moving to Santa Rosa meant navigating cratered roads and driving 14 kilometers just to buy groceries. Today, the quiet frontier is ground zero for a heavyweight retail clash among the nation’s wealthiest dynasties.

In 1996, when our family packed up our life in Makati and headed south to Santa Rosa, Laguna, our friends assumed we had either discovered inner peace or lost our minds. Back then, the Sta. Rosa–Tagaytay corridor was neither the bustling suburban haven nor the commercial goldmine it is today.

The lone imposing landmark was Laguna Technopark—then spanning 224 hectares, though it has since more than doubled to 471. Otherwise, the road was an unsparing ribbon of dirt and asphalt, pockmarked with axle-busting potholes that punished car suspensions and tested our family’s faith in country living.

Our nearest proper pantry was South Supermarket in Balibago, a 14-kilometer expedition that took over 45 minutes one-way because of cratered roads. With the first Skyway under construction, having our driver shuttle my wife and me to our Makati offices—and our toddler daughter to Kumon—routinely consumed close to six punishing hours.
We paid for green horizons in the quiet currency of endless patience, with daily life easing only slightly when the Campos Group opened Paseo de Santa Rosa in 1998.

blocks.caption: GREENFIELD. Bird’s eye view of Paseo Outlets, Greenfields City, Santa Rosa, Laguna. Courtesy of Greenfields Development Corp.

blocks.text: Three decades later, that quiet frontier has transformed into the most fiercely contested retail prize in Southern Luzon.

On November 27, SM Prime Holdings will open SM Nuvali. Boasting over 82,000 square meters of gross leasable area, a one-hectare indoor garden, and a tenant mix heavily weighted toward dining, it will debut as Laguna’s largest SM mall.

blocks.caption: ‘Cookie-cutter’ no more? SM Nuvali to open November 27 with 1-hectare indoor garden

blocks.text: Yet the true significance is not merely its footprint, but its audacious geography. SM is planting its flag squarely inside Nuvali—the 2,290-hectare estate Ayala Land spent nearly two decades transforming into the province’s commercial epicenter.

To casual observers, SM is invading Ayala turf. But in property development, this looks more like an Ayala masterstroke: Ayala monetized prime estate land at peak commercial valuations—where lots along this corridor command upwards of P100,000 per square meter—turning its biggest rival into both a paying buyer and a massive foot-traffic generator for Nuvali itself.

Nor is Ayala retreating to the sidelines. In response, Ayala Malls Nuvali (formerly Solenad) has put its own expansion into full throttle, evolving into a Super Regional Mall. By adding over 50,000 square meters of retail space, Ayala will push its footprint past 100,000 square meters to accommodate 550 stores. With Phase 1 opening in late 2026 and Phase 2 adding a two-story food hall, wellness destinations, and a chapel, Ayala is meeting SM’s arrival with overwhelming scale of its own. For those of us who once spent half a day hunting down butter and eggs, watching these two titans collide in our backyard feels surreal.

Just down the road, another subtle yet pivotal drama is unfolding. Inside Vista Mall Santa Rosa, Manny Villar’s AllDay Supermarket has bowed out after nearly a decade, replaced by the Gokongwei group’s Shopwise. At first glance, it looks like routine tenant rotation. In reality, it marks the first visible breach in the Villar group’s signature closed-loop strategy. (READ: Some suppliers get short end of stick as Villars keep winning)

Vista Mall was hardly dropped into unfamiliar territory. The Villars had planted deep residential roots nearby through Brittany’s Georgia Club and Augusta, alongside Crown Asia’s Valenza. The formula was classic vertical integration: buy a Villar home, furnish it at AllHome, and fill the grocery cart at AllDay so household spending never left the ecosystem.

That fortress is now showing undeniable, ugly cracks. AllDay’s revenue slipped from P10.19 billion to P9.25 billion in 2024, with net income retreating to P268 million, amid selective store closures and delayed financial reporting among Villar-linked listed entities. Surrendering a flagship anchor occupied since 2016 looks less like routine rotation and more like a pragmatic corporate retreat.

Shopwise’s arrival is a retail salvage mission for floor space and foot traffic that AllDay could no longer afford to tie down. By installing an established grocer, Vista Mall sacrifices family insularity to become a more durable, traffic-friendly landlord. The irony is inescapable: a Villar mall may now become stronger precisely by depending less on Villar retail.
The Gokongweis, meanwhile, are hardly strangers here. Robinsons Supermarket anchors Solenad 2, while another Shopwise already draws shoppers at Greenfield City’s Laguna Central.
For Robinsons Retail, moving into Vista Mall secures immediate, low-friction access to the affluent Santa Rosa–Nuvali belt without developing an estate from scratch or carrying Villar corporate risk.
Yet if Shopwise succeeds where AllDay faltered, the contrast will be telling: two supermarket operators tested under identical conditions, on the very same tile floors.
With that move, four of the country’s most powerful corporate dynasties—Ayala, SM, Villar, and Gokongwei—are converging on a single corridor to fight over our household wallets.

To equity analysts, this is a clash of corporate models: Ayala’s integrated ecosystem versus SM’s retail gravity, alongside a repositioned Villar mall leaning on Gokongwei merchandising. But for those of us watching from our front gates, this is the tangible story of suburban decentralization in motion. Backed by the Cavite Laguna Expressway(CALAX) and rapid sprawl, Santa Rosa alone has expanded past 430,000 residents, pulling in disposable income from Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, Silang, and Tagaytay.

The tycoons can landscape their atriums, refine their tenant mixes, and deploy their billions. But out here, where axle-snapping ruts have given way to an embarrassment of retail riches, real power no longer resides in Makati boardrooms.

It rests with the long-suffering suburbanites who paved the way. The empires will build, but ordinary families like ours will pick the ultimate victors—one grocery cart, one restaurant bill, and one weekend errand at a time. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
articles.summary: Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.

image.caption: Rebel groups had seized control of airports and sections of Tigray's capital on September 23Image: AFP

blocks.text: Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.
Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.
"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.
Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.
Return to civil war?
Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict

The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.
The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.

The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.
Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.
The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.
Fears of wider regional unrest
The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.
For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.
Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.
The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

articles.title: No bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fans
articles.summary:
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their team

  • Get our
articles.byline: Australian Associated Press and Andrew Messenger

blocks.text: A driver whose car careered into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters – leaving children as young as five injured – will be kept in custody as the community rallies to support those hospitalised after the crash.
Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout on Saturday morning.

Six people remain at the John Hunter hospital with injuries caused by the collision, according to the Hunter New England Local Health District chief executive, Tracey McCosker. Two are in a serious condition, while four are stable.
They include a five-year-old girl who had been placed into an induced coma with critical injuries, although her condition has stabilised.

Samarasinghe was taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences, including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.
He did not make any application for release during a brief court appearance on Sunday, and he was formally refused bail. The judge also endorsed a warrant for a health assessment.
The bail court was told the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carried a maximum jail term of seven years.
He will next appear at the Newcastle local court on 15 October.

Chris Clancy was among those injured in the crash, after joining thousands of Newcastle Knights fans to lined the streets to farewell their team as the players travelled to Sydney for the grand final.
“We’re there at the roundabout having fun – cars going past, beeping their horns, people waving,” Clancy said.
“The next thing, this car stops [at] the roundabout and then he just floored it on the wet ground, lost it.
“It happened in seconds, but when you stand there, seeing the car coming at you, I honestly thought I was going to die. It just felt like slow motion.”
Clancy suffered small fractures in his ribs and spine, a broken collarbone, and small fractures in his foot.
after newsletter promotion
Investigators did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was being driven erratically before the crash.
Multiple fundraisers have been established for the victims of the incident, including one for the five-year-old girl and another for Wallsend grandfather Dave Martin.
Martin was injured after being struck by the car while trying to protect his two young granddaughters, sustaining multiple fractures in both legs and undergoing a lengthy surgery.
He was known in Wallsend for his love of the Knights, often decorating his barber shop on Nelson Street with team paraphernalia.
The Knights’ chief executive, Peter Parr, expressed deep concern for those affected by the crash.
“Newcastle is a strong community,” he said.
“We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most.”

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is providing parenting effectiveness service to families amid the recent school violence incidents across the country.
DSWD spokesperson Irene Dumlao said the service will strengthen parents in their parental responsibilities.

"Ang mahalaga dito ay 'yung na pro-provide na parenting effectiveness service para mas mapalakas pa ang ugnayan ng pamilya, and for the parents na mapalakas 'yung pag-perform nila ng parental responsibilities," Dumlao told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.
(What's important is that the parenting effectiveness service can help strengthen the relationships in a family and the parents' capabilities to perform their parental responsibilities.)

"Ibig sabihin, sa loob ng tahanan, napakalakas na ang ugnayan at ang relasyon para magabayan nang magabayan nang husto ng mga magulang ang kanilang mga anak ng sa gayon mailayo sila sa kapahamakan o karahasan," she added
(This means strengthening relationships and communication within the home so that parents can properly guide their children, help them make better decisions, and protect them from harm or violence.)
A Grade 11 student was wounded after being stabbed by a fellow student at a school in Laoag City on Friday. The incident involved teenagers believed to have a confrontation.
In June, two students opened fire on their classmates at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, killing three students and injuring 20 others.
In August, a student shot his classmate at Ateneo de Zamboanga University before turning the gun on himself, leading to two deaths.
Dumlao shared that DSWD also provides psychosocial first aid to affected individuals who have witnessed incidents of violence.
The agency also provides capacity building for trauma care so that other individuals in the school can observe the behaviors of affected people.
Dumlao said DSWD's social workers are assessing affected families to determine what assistance the department will provide. —KG, GMA News
