articles.title: Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son
articles.summary:
President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades

The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.

Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.

“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”

blocks.caption: Lula led a campaign march through central Rio de Janeiro, travelling from Candelária toward Cinelândia. Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.

“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.
Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”
From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.

blocks.caption: Lula, who is seeking re-election, used the the march to mobilise supporters two days before voters head to the polls on 4 October 2026. Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.
The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.

Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.

blocks.caption: Two Lula supporters.  Photograph: António Lacerda/EPA

blocks.text: Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.

“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.

Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”

blocks.caption: Supporters of the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, at Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years. Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters

blocks.text: Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”
Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.

“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”

During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.
Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.

“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.

Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they ​do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”

Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.

In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.

articles.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.summary: The coordinated release is aimed at heading off further price spikes and avoiding a ban on US diesel exports.

blocks.text: The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.
President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
articles.summary: Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to…

image.caption: Parliamentarians voted with a crowd of protesters outside awaiting the resultsImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Spain's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing.

Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through.

Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week, including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus.
Why and how did the emergency decrees fail?
Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate.
Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think."

blocks.caption: Sanchez tried to rally majority support for the measures at the last in parliament, but could not succeed Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures.

The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172.
The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166.
Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply.
Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government.

blocks.caption: Rising rents were a sensitive issue in Spain for years, but one particularly emotive eviction brought it to the boilImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did protesters say after the vote?
The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike.
"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike."

The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen Abascal has since been granted a reprieve, but the more widespread attempts to improve the situation remain stalled for nowImage: Francesco Militello Mirto/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How tough is Spain's housing market?
The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs.

Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30.

"People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday.

The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament.

articles.title: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
articles.summary: More than 550 schools have been disrupted as protests over standards and lack of teachers continue.

blocks.text: On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
In Marseille, fireworks were thrown at police and teachers were also inadvertently splashed with petrol at a school there, officials said.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes had suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government.
"We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house, so," she told AFP.
"We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of who were children - had been taken into custody.
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."

articles.title: "NAZA": Israeli military issues statement on film
articles.summary: The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."

image.caption: Still from the documentary "NAZA"Image: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: When it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in mid-September, "NAZA" received a 25-minute-long standing ovation and the Special Jury Prize. But in Israel, the documentary has fueled heated debate.

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar described the work of filmmakers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham "treason against the state" and urged that their citizenship be revoked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also sharply criticized the documentary.

Now the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has also rejected the film's allegations about its conduct during the war in Gaza. In a multi-page document, the military accuses the filmmakers of presenting a "distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture." The film, it says, is based on "substantial factual errors" resulting from "manipulative misrepresentations of reality."
An insider's look at the war

The 80-minute documentary examines the Israel Defense Forces' operations during the war in Gaza. It is based on interviews conducted with 24 anonymous military and intelligence personnel, who describe internal procedures and decision-making processes involved in selecting targets in the Gaza Strip. According to the interviewees, high civilian casualty estimates were, in some cases, deliberately factored into these decisions.

The IDF rejects those claims. It says it has never planned or carried out attacks while anticipating hundreds of civilian deaths. It also disputes the film's claim that artificial intelligence selected targets without human oversight, saying people have always made decisions about targets and attacks.

The military also accuses the filmmakers of omitting important facts. According to the IDF, the film fails to show the role of military legal advisors and commanders in reviewing and authorizing attacks or the measures it says it takes to protect civilians. It also argues that the film does not adequately address the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,200 people were killed and 250 people were taken hostage.

Several human rights organizations and a UN commission have accused Israel of committing acts of genocide in Gaza. According to health authorities in Gaza and other sources, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began.
'NAZA' opens in theaters worldwide

Speaking at the awards ceremony in Venice in mid-September, co-director Yuval Abraham said: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist. That is why it's really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film."
Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham also worked on the film "No Other Land," which won an Oscar for Best Documentary Feature in 2025.
Israeli leaders condemn acclaimed Gaza documentary 'NAZA'

"NAZA" comes from the Hebrew term "Nezek Agavi," meaning collateral damage. According to a soldier interviewed in the film, the acronym is used within the military to refer to the estimated number of civilians who could be killed in an attack.

Numerous human rights organizations, including the Israeli group B'Tselem, have expressed their support for the filmmakers. After its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, "NAZA" is now showing in theaters worldwide.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Aviation security back in spotlight after nightmare on flydubai flight to Israel
articles.summary:
Questions raised over cockpit locks and screening of pilots as UAE investigates details and motives of near disaster

At around 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her…

blocks.text: At around 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter Nina to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.

Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he didn’t react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.

Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.
Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”
Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.

As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in around a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.

Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.
In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.
The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”

For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.

In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.

Experts said there had been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.

In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.

Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.

“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”

blocks.caption: People disembark from a flydubai plane carrying Israeli passengers from the disrupted flight at Ben Gurion international airport near Tel Aviv. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive end with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.

Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.

“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane is the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”

There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.

blocks.caption: A passenger with blood on his T-shirt onboard the flydubai plane. Photograph: Amit Segal

blocks.text: There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.
Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”

Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.

The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.

Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.

Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

articles.title: US Coast Guard says it has intercepted ship carrying fuel to Cuba
articles.summary:
US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues

The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship…

blocks.text: The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound for Cuba, as the ⁠Trump administration’s crippling ⁠oil embargo against ​the island nation continued.

The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in the Caribbean Sea between Cuba ⁠and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship ⁠was 91 metres (300ft) long.
“Grace was transiting to Cuba, carrying fuel, ​and was believed to be employing ‌tactics common amongst the ‌dark fleet,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.

A Coast Guard team ‌boarded the ship and escorted it to Mexico, where a Mexican navy inspection team “confirmed the presence of large quantities of fuel in the vessel’s ballast tanks”. The vessel was also carrying several containers believed to contain illicit fuel, the statement said.

The Trump administration has openly stated ‌that its goal is to change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put the country ​under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

Oil shipments from Cuba’s traditional suppliers, Venezuela and Mexico, ended abruptly after the US ousted the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. US Coast Guard ⁠cutters patrol the waters off Cuba, while sanctions and threats have dissuaded ​tankers from even ​setting sail.

“The high seas ​are not a sanctuary for lawlessness,” Adm Kevin Lunday, the commandant ​of the Coast ‌Guard, said. “Dark fleet ​actors who employ ​deceptive tactics to engage in illicit activities will not evade justice.”
The statement did not say how authorities knew the fuel was headed to Cuba or how much fuel Grace was carrying.

articles.title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll
articles.summary:
Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on…

blocks.text: India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.

The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.

Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.

blocks.caption: Abhijeet Dipke addresses supporters in Mumbai on Friday. Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.

blocks.caption: Supporters of the All India Students Association demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar at a protest in Bengaluru. Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.

The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.

“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”

Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
after newsletter promotion
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.

blocks.caption: A demonstrator holding a placard wears a mask depicting the face of Gyanesh Kumar. Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

blocks.text: The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared ​aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.

Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.

Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.

Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election ​commission office in Delhi next week.

articles.title: Germany's Franz Reindl elected new IIHF president
articles.summary: Franz Reindl has been elected president of ice hockey's world governing body. The former forward was a member of West Germany's Olympic bronze medal-winning team.

image.caption: Franz Reindl's term as IIHF president runs until 2030 Image: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: Franz Reindl came from behind to narrowly beat Petr Briza of the Czech Republic in a run-off vote to become the International Ice Hockey Federation's new president on Friday.

Reindl had trailed Briza 48-36 in the first round of voting but picked up crucial votes after Aivaz Omorkanov of Kyrgyzstan was eliminated. He then beat Briza 60-57 in the runoff held on the Spanish island of Tenerife. Six of a total of nine candidates had withdrawn prior to the election.

The 71-year-old German, who had been a member of the IIHF Council since 2016, succeeds Canadian-born Frenchman Luc Tardif, who had announced in March that he would not seek a further term in office. Reindl's election comes 5 years after he had finished as runner-up to Tardif. His term runs until 2030.
Wealth of experience

Reindl has done it all in German ice hockey, having been a player and coach, as well as serving as the first CEO of the top-flight professional league, the Deutsche Eishockey Liga (DEL), from 1994 to 96. He also headed the organizing committees for three World Championships – in 2001, 2010 and 2017. From 2014 to 2022 he served as president of the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB), overseeing an upturn in the fortunes of the men's national team, who won the silver medal at the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics in 2018.

blocks.caption: Franz Reindl served as interim coach of the men's national team, here during the 2004 World Cup of hockey Image: Christof Koepsel/Bongarts/Getty Images

blocks.text: "Franz Reindl has shaped German ice hockey for decades—as a player, but above all through the various key roles he has held within our federation," the current DEB chairman, Frank Lutz, said.
"The fact that the international ice hockey family is now entrusting him with the leadership of the IIHF is a great tribute to his work."
Successful playing career

Like Briza, who was a goalie for the Czechoslovakia team that won bronze in Albertville in 1992, Reindl was also an Olympic bronze medalist, having been a member of the 1976 West Germany team who beat the United States and Finland to finish third in Lake Placid.
Domestically, Reindl played 669 games and scored 423 goals for SC Riessersee and SB Rosenheim over 16 seasons in the Eishockey-Bundesliga, the predecessor to the DEL.

Tardif's years as IIHF president were marked by two major events; the return of National Hockey League players to the Olympic tournament in Milan Cortina this year, and the exclusion from international play of Russia in 2022 over the country's full-scale war on neighboring Ukraine.
Reindl is the second German to be elected IIHF president after Günter Sabetzki, who held the post from 1975 to 1994.

articles.title: Climate leaders called for solar energy for 'everyone, everywhere' by 2030, but with three years to go, is that goal attainable?
articles.summary: Prominent climate leaders have called on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to make a push for solar power before the decade is out, repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.…

image.caption: The open letter calls for solar for all, everywhere — particularly for those who don't have access to electricityImage: Tsvangirayi Mukwazhi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a world "set ablaze by war and warming," with ever-worsening climate disasters such as wildfires in Europe and collapsing glaciers in Nepal, solar energy provides a solution in the form of clean, affordable power, prominent climate leaders wrote in an open letter.

Signed by author Bill McKibben, former UN Climate Secretary Christiana Figueres and Canada's former Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna, the letter makes a clear call. It urges governments, businesses, institutions and the public to come together to provide clean, affordable energy to "everyone, everywhere by 2030" — from the close to one billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

blocks.caption: Close to 1 billion people don't have access to reliable electricity — solar power could change thatImage: Moritz Wolf/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: With just a little over three years to go until the decade is out, how realistic is this push?
"It's an ambitious target, but we've blown away in terms of where we thought we would be on solar and renewables," McKenna told DW. "So let's just keep on going."
Where are we currently with solar?

According to global energy think tank Ember,solar power has grown at its highest rate in eight years. In 2025, it increased by a record 30% over the previous year and has risen more than tenfold since 2015.

Solar is the cheapest form of electricity in the history of the world, said McKenna, who founded the climate advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, and the global coalition Women Leading on Climate.
"It is scaling way faster than anyone ever imagined."
As is battery technology used to store excess renewable energy.

"The cost of batteries have as well come down as the cost of solar modules," said Eicke Weber, a physicist and former director of Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems who went on to found the European Solar Manufacturing Council, among other things.
"We have the technologies available and we have enough money to finance it," he said, of a transition to widespread solar access.
In 2025, for the first time in 100 years, renewable energy sources overtook coal power in the global electricity mix, Ember's most recent analysis showed.
Where do we need to get to with solar?
At the moment, installed solar capacity around the world stands at 3 terawatts. 1TW equals 1000 gigawatts, and a single nuclear power plant has a capacity of 1GW.

Currently, the world produces about 1TW of new photovoltaic capacity each year, most of it in China. Weber says in order to fully change global energy supply to renewables, we would need about 50TW, adding that "we have more production capacities than we are selling."
Roughly 655 million people still lack accessto electricity.
"The pace of electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa has to triple to achieve universal access by 2030," McKenna said, pointing out how quickly this gap could be closed with solar.

Areas without electricity have the opportunity to leapfrog straight into clean technologies, she says, bypassing the fossil fuels that are heating the planet. Rising global temperatures are fueling extreme weather events such as drought, storms and flooding around the world.

"And there's a misunderstanding, which is often propagated intentionally by fossil fuel companies, that it's expensive, it's hard, it's unreliable. And that just isn't the case anymore," she said. "To be honest, the most unreliable thing is if you're trying to pass fossil fuels through the Strait of Hormuz."
Is solar for all, everywhere really doable in that short amount of time?

Hans-Josef Fell is used to the argument that certain things cannot be done. Widely known as a pioneer of renewable energy, he drafted Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act, which established feed-in tariffs that catalyzed clean energy growth at home and beyond.

"The Renewable Energy Sources Act unleashed exponential growth that shattered every assumption about what was achievable. It overturned the scenarios and projections that policymakers and experts had considered realistic. In the end, reality outperformed all expectations," said Fell, who now heads the think tank Energy Watch Group.

Fell, who has lived off grid for five years, said achieving a global energy transition requires political and societal will that is "currently lacking around the world because public debate is dominated by fossil fuel interests."

blocks.caption: Solar power has been growing exponentially over the past yearsImage: Thomas Imo/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to calculations by his think tank, if global energy demand were met entirely by renewables, solar energy would account for roughly 60-70% of the supply. The rest would come from wind power, and other sources, such as bioenergy and hydropower.
Where to go from here?
Countries like China and Pakistan have already pushed ahead.
"It is in our hands right now in the year 2026 to say we drop everything, we concentrate on this problem. We don't need to wait for new research," Weber said.
"It is possible to achieve this, but it would require a very kind of moonshot program," he added, saying it would need serious political backing.

He says while it might be possible for Germany to pull off such as transition in two or three years, if the political will were there, it would likely take longer to achieve on a global scale. "We would need probably till 2040 to say that we have a goal of a worldwide 80%, 90% electricity from renewables."
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions

"I would sum it up this way: If we as a global society tackle this properly, we might actually be able to make it happen," Fell said. "And even if we achieve only 90% of that goal, it would still be a remarkable accomplishment."
McKenna pointed to the need for blended finance, calling on governments, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the private sector to put in money.
"What is irrational is continuing down the road of fossil fuels," she added. "That's irrational on the costs, the risks, the impacts. It's an old technology."

articles.title: U.A.E. says co-pilot on FlyDubai plane that nearly crashed attacked captain with cockpit's crash axe

image.caption: Passengers embark on a FlyDubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, on Wednesday. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the plane.
The co-pilot tried to take control of the plane in a 'terrorist attack,' U.A.E. prosecutor general says

The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight before passengers and others stopped the attack is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, said on Saturday.
The United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the captain with the cockpit's crash axe and tried to take control of the plane in a "terrorist attack."

"Investigations into the incident involving FlyDubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in a statement carried by the U.A.E's state news agency.

The prosecutor general's comments were the first by Emirati investigators to describe the incident as an attempted terrorist attack. While Emirati authorities and the airline have not publicly identified the co-pilot, Israeli officials have previously said he is an Omani national.

items: 'Prepared ourselves for the worst': FlyDubai passenger recounts moments during cockpit attack

blocks.text: All three people who identified the co-pilot spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The Gulf diplomat said investigations are underway to establish whether he acted as a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."

The co-pilot, who officials said nearly crashed the sharply plummeting flight with more than 170 people aboard, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a separate person familiar with the matter said.

The co-pilot was then hired by the U.A.E-based airline FlyDubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman's barring of him was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
An official says the co-pilot was born in the U.A.E

How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don't maintain diplomatic relations with it. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
There was no immediate comment from the U.A.E government or Oman Air. Oman's government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
FlyDubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said on Saturday.
The co-pilot was born in the U.A.E and his mother is Syrian, according to another regional official with knowledge of the investigation.
'I can't let anyone die': FlyDubai pilot tells Indian PM how he managed to open cockpit door

The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman's national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.

Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot's motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.

items: What we know so far about the midair FlyDubai attack

blocks.text: U.A.E senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a "dangerous terrorist act" in a post on X. The incident is a test for the U.A.E government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot's background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radicalization," but provided no evidence.
How FlyDubai Flight 1073 survived impossible odds | About That

The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.
Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the U.A.E as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
An Israeli government official confirmed that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the U.A.E-led investigation.

The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the U.A.E. to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israeli travellers. Most passengers aboard the plane were Israeli nationals.
Once crew and passengers intervened, the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
articles.summary: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos…

image.caption: Sheikh Mansour, as he is widely known, fronted the deal to buy City for the UAE nearly 20 years agoImage: Martin Rickett/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Manchester City has won the English Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. Whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high-profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs." These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Der Spiegel, a German magazine, and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continues to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a club statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."
On Friday, the club issued a further statement saying it had lodged a "comprehensive Appeal."
What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off the books, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. The report says all this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Although the Premier League, the world's most commercially successful football league, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point out that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to take action. The report shows that Manchester City, which had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.
Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour, fronted the takeover. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds several government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation-state ownership of this type is controversial in European football. Manchester City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain, which Qatar owned and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United, which is owned 85% by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

blocks.caption: As well as huge domestic success, City won the Champions League under Pep Guardiola in 2022-23Image: Jose Breton/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.
How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big-money transfers after the UAE investment arrived. At the time, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA introduced its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules for the 2011-12 season, while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relatively low commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club was handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with these financial rules, City set up a system they called "Project Longbow" in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine, but one arm of it was an agreement with a third party called Fordham that was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money into their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.
What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. So far, no sanctions have been imposed on City, and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile, the club, which is top of the Premier League, faces Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have previously fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5 million breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the Premier League does not operate England's second-tier league, the Championship.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.
This article was originally published on September 30, 2026. It was updated on October 2, 20206 with Manchester City's statement confirming that it had lodged an appeal.

articles.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
articles.summary:
Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over…
articles.byline: Megan Davies and James Michelin for MetDesk

blocks.text: Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.

Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.

Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.

blocks.caption: A woman and child displaced by flash floods and mudslides in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.

This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.

Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.

The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
articles.summary:
Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about Pharaohs’ origins

On the…

blocks.text: On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

blocks.caption: Volunteer Razan Mujahid works on the mural. Photograph: Rasmet Basma

blocks.text: The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

blocks.caption: The mural has reignited a debate about the complexion of ancient Egyptians. Photograph: Rasmet Basma

blocks.text: This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”

Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.

blocks.caption: The mural was repainted white just hours before President Xi landed in Egypt. Photograph: Hanaa Hammad

blocks.text: “That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.

“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.
